data.title: Fenfluramine as antiseizure medication for epilepsy.
data.abstract: Fenfluramine hydrochloride has classically been described as acting pharmacologically through a serotonergic mechanism. Therefore, it was initially used as an anorectic drug, given that impaired serotonin homeostasis may be associated with increased food intake. Although positive results were documented, cardiovascular concerns resulted in its temporary withdrawal. Nevertheless, a novel role in patients with epilepsy was later suggested by isolated clinical observations. The wide application of genetic testing allowed the classification (predominantly as Dravet syndrome) of patients in whom benefit was seen, while with the development of zebrafish models, its antiepileptic properties were confirmed at a molecular level. Data from randomized clinical trials have shown a beneficial effect of fenfluramine, as an adjunct therapy, on seizure control for children with Dravet syndrome, though there is still uncertainty about the impact on neurodevelopment in these patients. No signs of heart valve disease have been documented to date. Long-term and appropriately designed clinical studies will verify whether fenfluramine is a therapeutic agent of high importance, living up to the promise shown so far. What this paper adds Fenfluramine is a very promising repurposed therapy specifically for seizures in Dravet syndrome. The long-term effect of fenfluramine on neurodevelopmental prognosis requires further investigation.

data.title: Efficacy and safety of adjunctive antiseizure medications for dravet syndrome: A systematic review and network meta-analysis.
data.abstract: Purpose: Recently, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved stiripentol, cannabidiol, and fenfluramine to treat patients with Dravet syndrome (DS). Moreover, soticlestat was determined as a promising new drug for the treatment of DS as it has good efficacy and safety. However, the efficacy and safety of these drugs have not yet been evaluated in "head-to-head" trials. This study aimed to compare and evaluate the efficacy and safety of these adjunctive antiseizure medications in the treatment of DS. Methods: We searched in PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science databases for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and open-label extension (OLE) studies in patients with DS. We performed a random-effect meta-analysis of OLE studies and a network meta-analysis for RCTs to evaluate the efficacy and safety of antiseizure medications in the treatment of DS. Primary efficacy outcomes were defined as a ≥50% reduction in seizure frequency compared with baseline. Furthermore, safety evaluation indicators were defined as the incidence of adverse events (AEs) and serious adverse events (SAEs) during treatment. Relative ranking was assessed using the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) probabilities. Results: Seven RCTs involving four antiseizure medications (stiripentol, cannabidiol, fenfluramine, and soticlestat) and a total of 634 patients were included in the analysis. According to the SUCRA results, all four drugs significantly reduced the frequency of seizures compared with the placebo. Soticlestat was the most likely to reduce seizure frequency by ≥50% compared to the baseline [risk ratio (RR): 19.32; 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.20-311.40], followed by stiripentol and fenfluramine. Stiripentol was ranked highest for the near percentage reduction in the seizure rate from baseline [RR: 12.33; 95% CI: 1.71-89.17] and the occurrence of any treatment-emergent adverse events [RR: 3.73; 95% CI: 1.65-8.43] and serious adverse events [RR: 4.76; 95% CI: 0.61-37.28]. A total of ten OLE studies containing 1,121 patients were included in our study. According to the results of the meta-analysis, the order of probability of reducing seizure frequency by ≥50% was fenfluramine (0.715, 95% CI: 0.621-0.808), stiripentol (0.604, 95% CI: 0.502-0.706), cannabidiol (0.448, 95% CI: 0.403-0.493). And the probability of occurrence of AEs is ranked as fenfluramine(0.832, 95% CI: 0.795-0.869), cannabidiol (0.825, 95% CI:0.701-0.950), stiripentol (0.823, 95% CI: 0.707-0.938), soticlestat (0.688, 95% CI: 0.413-0.890). Conclusion: According to the results of indirect comparison of efficacy and safety, cannabidiol is slightly inferior to the other three antiseizure medications in terms of efficacy and safety. Soticlestat, fenfluramine, and stripentol may have little difference in efficacy, but soticlestat and fenfluramine are safer. Soticlestat is probably the best adjunctive antiseizure medication, followed by fenfluramine. This conclusion is consistent with the comparison of long-term efficacy and safety.

data.title: Fenfluramine significantly reduces day-to-day seizure burden by increasing number of seizure-free days and time between seizures in patients with Dravet syndrome: A time-to-event analysis.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVE
The number, unpredictability, and severity of seizures experienced by patients with Dravet syndrome (DS) negatively impact quality of life (QOL) for patients, caregivers, and families. Metrics are needed to assess whether patients with residual seizures have moved meaningfully toward seizure freedom after treatment with new antiseizure medications.
METHODS
We evaluated the time required postrandomization for each patient to experience the same number of seizures experienced during baseline (i.e., time-to-nth seizure), using a post hoc time-to-event (TTE) analysis of data from two Phase 3 placebo-controlled trials of adjunctive fenfluramine for DS (Study 1, N = 119; Study 2, N = 87). Patients aged 2-19 years were randomized to placebo or adjunctive fenfluramine (Study 1: .7 mg/kg/day or .2 mg/kg/day; Study 2: .4 mg/kg/day with stiripentol). Data were analyzed by Kaplan-Meier TTE curves and waterfall plots.
RESULTS
The proportion of patients who never reached baseline seizure frequency was greater with fenfluramine than with placebo (Study 1: fenfluramine .7 mg/kg/day, 60%; fenfluramine .2 mg/kg/day, 31%; placebo, 13%; Study 2: fenfluramine .4 mg/kg/day, 58%; placebo, 2%). Median time-to-nth seizure was longer after fenfluramine than after placebo (Study 1: fenfluramine .7 mg/kg/day, 13 weeks; .2 mg/kg/day, 10 weeks; placebo, 7 weeks; Study 2: fenfluramine .4 mg/kg/day, 13 weeks; placebo, 5 weeks; p < .001). Longest duration of convulsive seizure-free days was increased in active groups versus the placebo group (Study 1: fenfluramine .7 and .2 mg/kg/day, 25.0 and 15.0 days; placebo, 9.5 days [p = .0001; p = .0352]; Study 2: fenfluramine .4 mg/kg/day, 22.0 days; placebo, 13.0 days [p = .004]). The most common adverse events included decreased appetite, pyrexia, upper respiratory tract infection, diarrhea, and fatigue.
SIGNIFICANCE
These data demonstrate that fenfluramine can significantly reduce day-to-day seizure burden in patients with DS, providing prolonged periods of convulsive seizure-free days, which may help reduce the physical and emotional disease toll while improving health-related QOL for patients and caregivers.

data.title: Improved everyday executive functioning following profound reduction in seizure frequency with fenfluramine: Analysis from a phase 3 long-term extension study in children/young adults with Dravet syndrome.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVE
Individuals with Dravet syndrome (DS) experience frequent pharmacoresistant seizures beginning in infancy. Most exhibit poor neurodevelopmental outcomes including motor function difficulties, behavior problems, and cognitive impairment. Cognitive deficits in children with DS have been associated with seizure frequency and antiseizure medication (ASM) use. Recent research in children and young adults with DS has begun to examine the role of executive functions (EFs), as these include higher-order cognitive functions and may mediate the relationship between risk factors and cognitive impairment. Current conceptualizations, however, of EFs involve the broader self-regulation of cognitive, behavioral, and emotional domains. We explored relationships between reduction in convulsive seizure frequency and everyday EFs in a subset of children and young adults with DS treated with adjunctive fenfluramine for 1 year.
METHODS
This is a post-hoc analysis of data from children and young adults with Dravet syndrome aged 5-18 years who participated in a phase 3 randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial (core study) followed by completion of at least 1 year of fenfluramine treatment in an open-label extension (OLE) study. Eligible children and young adults started the OLE study at 0.2 mg/kg/day fenfluramine and were titrated to optimal seizure control and tolerability (maximum daily dose: 26 mg/day). Parents/caregivers documented convulsive seizure frequency per 28 days (i.e., monthly convulsive seizure frequency [MCSF]) by electronic diary. A parent/caregiver for each child also completed the Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function (BRIEF®) parent form, a questionnaire capturing parents'/caregivers' perceptions of everyday EF that was included as a safety measure to assess treatment-related adverse effects on EF during the trial. Ratings on BRIEF® were mapped to the current edition, the BRIEF®2 parent form, and were used to calculate T-scores for the Behavior Regulation Index (BRI), Emotion Regulation Index (ERI), Cognitive Regulation Index (CRI), and Global Executive Composite (GEC). Change in BRIEF®2 T-scores from baseline in the core study to Year 1 of the OLE study was calculated. Spearman's rho correlation coefficients assessed associations between change in BRIEF®2 indexes/composite T-scores and percentage change in MCSF. Children and young adults were divided into 2 groups based on percentage of MCSF reduction achieved from pre-randomization baseline in the core study to Year 1 of the OLE study: <50% and ≥50% MCSF reduction. Changes in the distribution of BRIEF®2 indexes/composite T-scores were compared between MCSF reduction groups using Mann-Whitney U tests. The proportions of children and young adults in these groups who showed clinically meaningful improvement in everyday EF, defined as Reliable Change Index (RCI) values ≥95% certainty relative to a reference population of neurotypically developing healthy volunteers, were then assessed by cross-tabulations and Somers' D tests (p ≤ 0.05). When there was a significant meaningful improvement in an index score, post-hoc analyses using the same statistical methods were conducted to evaluate the individual BRIEF®2 scales composing that index. Supplemental analyses examined the proportions of patients in MCSF reduction groups <25% and ≥75% who achieved clinically meaningful improvement or worsening in everyday EF using RCI values ≥95% certainty and ≥80% certainty, respectively, relative to the reference population.
RESULTS
At the time of analysis, 58 children and young adults (mean age: 11 ± 4 years) had reached OLE Year 1 of fenfluramine treatment with a 75% median percentage reduction in seizure frequency from pre-randomization baseline. Overall, there was a significant correlation between change in MCSF and change in BRIEF®2 T-scores for ERI (p = 0.008), but not for BRI, CRI, or GEC (p > 0.05). At OLE Year 1, 78% (n = 45) of total children/young adults had ≥50% MCSF reduction (50% [n = 29] achieved ≥75% MCSF reduction) and 22% (n = 13) of total children/young adults had <50% MCSF reduction (12% [n = 7] showed <25% MCSF reduction). The ≥50% MCSF reduction group was significantly more likely to achieve clinically meaningful improvement (RCI ≥ 95% certainty) in ERI (p = 0.002) and in CRI (p = 0.001) than the <50% MCSF reduction group. There were no significant differences in the proportions of children and young adults in the 2 MCSF reduction groups showing clinically meaningful worsening (RCI ≥ 80% certainty) on the BRIEF®2 indexes/composite.
SIGNIFICANCE
In children and young adults with DS, the magnitude of reduction in MCSF after long-term treatment with adjunctive fenfluramine was associated with clinically meaningful levels of improvement in everyday EF. Seventy-eight percent (78%) of children and young adults treated with adjunctive fenfluramine for 1 year in the OLE study achieved ≥50% reduction in MCSF, for a magnitude of efficacy associated with a significantly greater likelihood of experiencing clinically meaningful improvement in emotion regulation and cognitive regulation.

data.title: Fenfluramine responder analyses and numbers needed to treat: Translating epilepsy trial data into clinical practice.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVE
Clinical trials typically report antiepileptic drug efficacy by evaluating reduction in monthly convulsive seizure frequency (MCSF) through group response (active versus placebo). Although useful for regulatory purposes, population statistics do not easily translate into clinical practice, where treatment decisions are made on an individual-patient basis. Responder analyses help bridge this gap by showing proportions of patients who achieved various MCSF improvement levels. Deriving numbers needed to treat (NNTs) to achieve clinically desirable response levels can further inform individual decision-making. We calculated the NNT with fenfluramine to achieve "clinically meaningful" (≥50%) or "profound" (≥75%) MCSF reductions in patients with Dravet syndrome (DS).
METHODS
NNT to achieve ≥50% or ≥75% MCSF reduction was assessed using longitudinal data from two phase 3 studies for adjunctive fenfluramine in DS patients aged 2-18 years. NNT was calculated: 1/((Experimental-Responder Rate)-(Control-Responder Rate)).
RESULTS
In Study 1, NNTs to achieve ≥50% and ≥75% MCSF reduction were 1.8 and 2.1 at 0.7 mg/kg/day fenfluramine. In Study 2, these NNTs were 2.0 and 3.1, respectively. These results were seen as early as Weeks 6-7 and were sustained through Weeks 14-15.
INTERPRETATION
For every two to three patients with DS treated with fenfluramine in these trials, one patient achieved ≥50% or ≥75% MCSF reduction, respectively, compared with placebo (large treatment effect size; Cohen's d≈0.8). Responder analyses and NNTs can aid in clinical decision-making by offering clinically important information that is complementary to the population mean data on the chance of an individual patient achieving meaningful levels of MCSF improvement. (NCT02682927/NCT02826863, NCT02926898).

trajectory.final_answer:
# Key Question
In children with Dravet syndrome, how do cannabidiol (CBD) and fenfluramine compare regarding seizure frequency reduction and common adverse effects when used as add-on therapies?

## Efficacy on Seizure Frequency
Cannabidiol (CBD) has clear randomized evidence of reducing convulsive seizure frequency in Dravet syndrome. In the landmark double-blind, placebo-controlled NEJM trial, adjunctive CBD 20 mg/kg/day reduced median monthly convulsive seizures from 12.4 to 5.9, versus a decrease from 14.9 to 14.1 with placebo (adjusted difference −22.8 percentage points; 95% CI −41.1 to −5.4; P=0.01), with 43% achieving at least a 50% reduction versus 27% with placebo; overall condition improved on the caregiver global impression in 62% vs 34% of patients, and total seizures (all types) were reduced, though nonconvulsive seizures were not significantly affected <cite id="28538134">In the NEJM trial, adjunctive CBD 20 mg/kg/day reduced convulsive seizures from 12.4 to 5.9 per month versus 14.9 to 14.1 with placebo, yielding a −22.8 percentage point adjusted difference (P=0.01), with 43% versus 27% achieving at least a 50% reduction and improved caregiver global impression (62% vs 34%); total seizures decreased but nonconvulsive seizures did not significantly change</cite>. A subsequent JAMA dose-ranging RCT (GWPCARE2) showed both CBD 10 mg/kg/day and 20 mg/kg/day reduced convulsive seizures more than placebo, with percentage reductions from baseline of 48.7% (CBD10) and 45.7% (CBD20) versus 26.9% for placebo; responder rates were 48.7% and 45.7% for CBD10 and CBD20 vs 26.9% for placebo, with similar improvements on the Caregiver Global Impression of Change <cite id="32119035">In the JAMA dose-ranging trial, CBD 10 mg/kg/day and 20 mg/kg/day produced 48.7% and 45.7% reductions in convulsive seizure frequency versus 26.9% for placebo, with responder rates of 48.7% and 45.7% vs 26.9% and improved caregiver global impression</cite>.

For fenfluramine, two phase 3 RCTs (including one combined with stiripentol) demonstrated superior time-to-seizure metrics and greater seizure-free intervals versus placebo. In a post hoc time-to-event analysis, the proportion of patients who never reached baseline seizure frequency was higher with fenfluramine (Study 1: 0.7 mg/kg/day 60%, 0.2 mg/kg/day 31%) than placebo (13%), and median time to the same number of seizures was longer with fenfluramine (13 weeks for 0.7 mg/kg/day and 10 weeks for 0.2 mg/kg/day) versus 7 weeks with placebo; similar results were seen in Study 2 (fenfluramine 0.4 mg/kg/day 58% never reached baseline vs 2% with placebo; median time to nth seizure 13 vs 5 weeks), with increased longest seizure-free days (25.0 and 15.0 days for 0.7 and 0.2 mg/kg/day vs 9.5 days with placebo; 22.0 days vs 13.0 days with stiripentol combination) <cite id="34676542">In two phase 3 trials, fenfluramine (0.7 or 0.2 mg/kg/day) increased the proportion of patients who never reached baseline seizure frequency (60% and 31% vs 13% with placebo) and prolonged median time to nth seizure (13 and 10 weeks vs 7 weeks) and longest seizure-free days (25.0 and 15.0 days vs 9.5 days); in the stiripentol-combination study, fenfluramine 0.4 mg/kg/day similarly outperformed placebo (58% vs 2%) and achieved 22.0 vs 13.0 days of seizure-free days</cite>. Responder analyses across the fenfluramine trials indicate a large treatment effect: numbers needed to treat to achieve ≥50% monthly convulsive seizure reduction were approximately 1.8–2.0 overall, and about 2.0–3.1 to achieve ≥75% reduction, sustained from weeks 6–7 through 14–15 <cite id="33540241">Across two phase 3 fenfluramine trials, NNTs to achieve ≥50% and ≥75% monthly convulsive seizure reduction were 1.8–2.1 and 2.0–3.1, respectively, with effects evident by weeks 6–7 and sustained through 14–15</cite>. Long-term open-label extension data further showed that 78% of children/young adults achieved ≥50% reduction in monthly convulsive seizure frequency by year 1 on fenfluramine, with greater seizure reduction correlating with clinically meaningful improvements in everyday executive functioning <cite id="34023810">In a 1-year fenfluramine open-label extension, 78% of participants achieved ≥50% reduction in monthly convulsive seizure frequency, and greater seizure reduction correlated with clinically meaningful improvements in everyday executive functioning</cite>.

Comparative insights from a 2023 network meta-analysis (NMA) suggest that, among adjunctive antiseizure medications, fenfluramine has a higher probability of achieving a ≥50% seizure reduction than cannabidiol, while cannabidiol's discontinuation rate is lower than stiripentol's; the NMA also reported that cannabidiol had a lower odds of any adverse event than fenfluramine (OR 0.22, 95% CI 0.06–0.78), and that no statistically significant differences emerged for seizure freedom across agents <cite id="37695433">A 2023 NMA found fenfluramine had higher seizure response odds than cannabidiol (OR 14.07 vs 0.20 for stiripentol vs cannabidiol), with no significant differences in seizure freedom; cannabidiol had lower discontinuation than stiripentol and lower odds of any adverse event than fenfluramine (OR 0.22)</cite>. A broader pharmacology-focused review similarly characterizes fenfluramine as beneficial as adjunctive therapy in Dravet syndrome, with no documented heart valve disease to date, while emphasizing the need for long-term neurodevelopmental follow-up <cite id="33565102">A review notes randomized trials show adjunctive fenfluramine benefits in Dravet syndrome, with no documented heart valve disease and ongoing uncertainty about long-term neurodevelopmental effects</cite>. An additional Frontiers-in-Pharmacology NMA (2022) ranks fenfluramine among the top options for ≥50% seizure reduction and suggests it may be safer than cannabidiol and stiripentol, with soticlestat possibly superior for efficacy but overall results being indirect across trials <cite id="36120377">A 2022 NMA reported fenfluramine ranked high for ≥50% seizure reduction and appeared safer than cannabidiol and stiripentol, with soticlestat possibly best for efficacy but with indirect evidence across trials</cite>.

## Common Adverse Effects and Safety
With adjunctive CBD, the most frequent adverse events in randomized trials include gastrointestinal symptoms (diarrhea, vomiting), fatigue, pyrexia, and somnolence, with increased rates of abnormal liver-function tests and more treatment discontinuations compared with placebo in the NEJM trial; dose-ranging data show elevated liver transaminases more often at 20 mg/kg/day and five discontinuations due to adverse events in the higher-dose arm <cite id="28538134">In the NEJM trial, CBD more commonly caused diarrhea, vomiting, fatigue, pyrexia, somnolence, abnormal liver tests, and led to more withdrawals than placebo</cite> <cite id="32119035">In the JAMA dose-ranging trial, common adverse events were decreased appetite, diarrhea, somnolence, pyrexia, and fatigue; liver transaminases were elevated more often in the 20 mg/kg/day group and five patients discontinued due to adverse events</cite>. Systematic review data also indicate that cannabidiol had a lower proportion of any adverse events than fenfluramine in indirect comparisons (OR 0.22, 95% CI 0.06–0.78), and a lower discontinuation rate than stiripentol, though overall evidence quality was high and direct head-to-head safety comparisons remain limited <cite id="37695433">Across trials, cannabidiol had a lower odds of any adverse event and lower discontinuation than fenfluramine and stiripentol, respectively, though overall evidence quality was high and direct comparisons were indirect</cite>.

For fenfluramine, common adverse events in trials and long-term extension include decreased appetite, pyrexia, upper respiratory tract infections, diarrhea, and fatigue; cardiovascular concerns that prompted earlier withdrawal have not shown signs of heart valve disease in the Dravet-syndrome trials to date, although long-term cardiac safety continues to be monitored <cite id="34676542">In fenfluramine trials, common adverse events included decreased appetite, pyrexia, upper respiratory tract infection, diarrhea, and fatigue</cite> <cite id="33565102">Reviews note no documented heart valve disease with fenfluramine in Dravet syndrome trials and highlight the need for long-term cardiovascular safety monitoring</cite>. Network meta-analyses suggest fenfluramine may have a favorable safety profile relative to cannabidiol and stiripentol, though overall rankings are based on indirect comparisons and require confirmation in head-to-head studies <cite id="36120377">Network meta-analysis suggested fenfluramine may be safer than cannabidiol and stiripentol, but evidence is indirect and needs confirmation in head-to-head trials</cite>.

## Comparative Summary and Practical Implications
- Seizure reduction: Both agents reduce convulsive seizure frequency as adjuncts. CBD 20 mg/kg/day in NEJM reduced median monthly seizures by about 50% relative to placebo and achieved a 43% ≥50% responder rate; a dose-ranging trial showed CBD 10 mg/kg/day also produced clinically meaningful reductions. Fenfluramine phase 3 trials demonstrate superior time-to-seizure metrics and longer seizure-free intervals versus placebo, with responder analyses indicating NNTs around 2 for ≥50% reduction and around 3 for ≥75% reduction; long-term extension suggests sustained ≥50% reduction in roughly 78% by year 1 in real-world practice <cite id="28538134">CBD 20 mg/kg/day reduced convulsive seizures by about 50% versus placebo and achieved a 43% ≥50% responder rate</cite> <cite id="32119035">CBD 10 mg/kg/day also reduced seizures more than placebo in a dose-ranging trial</cite> <cite id="34676542">Fenfluramine prolonged time to seizures and increased seizure-free days versus placebo in phase 3 trials</cite> <cite id="33540241">Fenfluramine responder analyses showed NNTs of ~2 for ≥50% and ~3 for ≥75% reduction</cite> <cite id="34023810">By year 1, 78% achieved ≥50% reduction in monthly convulsive seizures on fenfluramine</cite>. Indirect comparative analyses suggest fenfluramine may have a higher probability of ≥50% reduction than cannabidiol, while cannabidiol's discontinuation rate is lower than stiripentol's; seizure freedom did not differ significantly across agents <cite id="37695433">Indirect comparisons suggest fenfluramine has higher seizure response odds than cannabidiol, cannabidiol has lower discontinuation than stiripentol, and no significant differences in seizure freedom across agents</cite>.
- Adverse effects: CBD more often causes gastrointestinal, fatigue, pyrexia, somnolence, and abnormal liver enzymes, with higher discontinuation rates than placebo in NEJM; dose 20 mg/kg/day had more liver enzyme elevations and some discontinuations. Fenfluramine commonly causes decreased appetite, pyrexia, upper respiratory infections, diarrhea, and fatigue, with no documented heart valve disease to date but requiring ongoing cardiovascular monitoring; NMAs suggest a lower odds of any adverse event compared with fenfluramine in indirect comparisons, though this may reflect trial context differences <cite id="28538134">CBD more frequently caused diarrhea, vomiting, fatigue, pyrexia, somnolence, abnormal liver tests, and more withdrawals than placebo</cite> <cite id="32119035">Liver transaminase elevations were more frequent at 20 mg/kg/day and five patients discontinued due to adverse events</cite> <cite id="34676542">Fenfluramine commonly caused decreased appetite, pyrexia, upper respiratory tract infection, diarrhea, and fatigue, with no documented heart valve disease to date</cite> <cite id="37695433">Cannabidiol had lower odds of any adverse event and lower discontinuation than fenfluramine in indirect comparisons</cite>.
- Limitations: Direct head-to-head RCTs of CBD versus fenfluramine in Dravet syndrome are limited; comparative estimates derive from NMAs and post hoc/time-to-event analyses, and long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes for fenfluramine and tolerability for CBD (e.g., liver toxicity) warrant ongoing monitoring and dedicated studies <cite id="33565102">Reviews emphasize the need for long-term neurodevelopmental follow-up with fenfluramine</cite> <cite id="28538134">Cannabidiol trials reported more abnormal liver tests and higher discontinuation than placebo, underscoring the need for monitoring</cite> <cite id="37695433">Network meta-analysis highlights high-quality evidence but indirect comparisons and the need for head-to-head trials</cite>.

## Bottom Line
- Seizure control: Both CBD and fenfluramine reduce seizure frequency as add-on therapies in Dravet syndrome, with fenfluramine trials showing favorable time-to-seizure and seizure-free interval metrics and responder analyses indicating NNTs around 2 for ≥50% reduction; CBD has robust responder rates and large reductions in convulsive seizures in RCTs. Comparative NMA suggests fenfluramine may achieve higher responder rates than CBD, though evidence is indirect <cite id="28538134">CBD 20 mg/kg/day reduced convulsive seizures by about 50% versus placebo and achieved a 43% ≥50% responder rate</cite> <cite id="32119035">CBD 10 mg/kg/day also reduced seizures more than placebo in a dose-ranging trial</cite> <cite id="34676542">Fenfluramine prolonged time to seizures and increased seizure-free days versus placebo in phase 3 trials</cite> <cite id="33540241">Fenfluramine responder analyses showed NNTs of ~2 for ≥50% and ~3 for ≥75% reduction</cite> <cite id="37695433">Indirect comparisons suggest fenfluramine has higher seizure response odds than cannabidiol</cite>.
- Adverse effects: CBD more often causes gastrointestinal, fatigue, pyrexia, somnolence, and liver enzyme abnormalities, with higher discontinuation than placebo; fenfluramine commonly causes decreased appetite, pyrexia, upper respiratory infections, diarrhea, and fatigue, with no documented heart valve disease to date but requiring cardiovascular monitoring; NMAs suggest fenfluramine has higher odds of any adverse event than cannabidiol in indirect comparisons <cite id="28538134">CBD more frequently caused diarrhea, vomiting, fatigue, pyrexia, somnolence, abnormal liver tests, and more withdrawals than placebo</cite> <cite id="32119035">Liver transaminase elevations were more frequent at 20 mg/kg/day and five patients discontinued due to adverse events</cite> <cite id="34676542">Fenfluramine commonly caused decreased appetite, pyrexia, upper respiratory tract infection, diarrhea, and fatigue, with no documented heart valve disease to date</cite> <cite id="37695433">Cannabidiol had lower odds of any adverse event than fenfluramine in indirect comparisons</cite>.

Overall, both agents are effective add-on therapies; selection should balance magnitude and durability of seizure reduction with adverse effect profiles and monitoring needs, recognizing the lack of direct head-to-head RCT data and the need for long-term neurodevelopmental and cardiovascular follow-up, particularly for fenfluramine and CBD-related liver toxicity <cite id="37695433">Comparative evidence is indirect and head-to-head trials are needed</cite> <cite id="33565102">Long-term neurodevelopmental effects of fenfluramine require further investigation</cite> <cite id="28538134">Cannabidiol was associated with higher rates of adverse events and more withdrawals than placebo in NEJM, underscoring monitoring needs</cite>.

<snippet id="32632153">Title: Pre-clinical study of induced pluripotent stem cell-derived dopaminergic progenitor cells for Parkinson's disease.
Authors: Doi, Daisuke, Magotani, Hiroaki, Kikuchi, Tetsuhiro et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: Nature communications
Abstract: Induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived dopaminergic (DA) neurons are an expected source for cell-based therapies for Parkinson's disease (PD). The regulatory criteria for the clinical application of these therapies, however, have not been established. Here we show the results of our pre-clinical study, in which we evaluate the safety and efficacy of dopaminergic progenitors (DAPs) derived from a clinical-grade human iPSC line. We confirm the characteristics of DAPs by in vitro analyses. We also verify that the DAP population include no residual undifferentiated iPSCs or early neural stem cells and have no genetic aberration in cancer-related genes. Furthermore, in vivo studies using immunodeficient mice reveal no tumorigenicity or toxicity of the cells. When the DAPs are transplanted into the striatum of 6-OHDA-lesioned rats, the animals show behavioral improvement. Based on these results, we started a clinical trial to treat PD patients in 2018.</snippet>
<snippet id="37438521">Title: Co-transplantation of autologous T reg cells in a cell therapy for Parkinson's disease.
Authors: Park, Tae-Yoon, Jeon, Jeha, Lee, Nayeon et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Nature
Abstract: The specific loss of midbrain dopamine neurons (mDANs) causes major motor dysfunction in Parkinson's disease, which makes cell replacement a promising therapeutic approach 1-4 . However, poor survival of grafted mDANs remains an obstacle to successful clinical outcomes 5-8 . Here we show that the surgical procedure itself (referred to here as 'needle trauma') triggers a profound host response that is characterized by acute neuroinflammation, robust infiltration of peripheral immune cells and brain cell death. When midbrain dopamine (mDA) cells derived from human induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells were transplanted into the rodent striatum, less than 10% of implanted tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) + mDANs survived at two weeks after transplantation. By contrast, TH - grafted cells mostly survived. Notably, transplantation of autologous regulatory T (T reg ) cells greatly modified the response to needle trauma, suppressing acute neuroinflammation and immune cell infiltration. Furthermore, intra-striatal co-transplantation of T reg cells and human-iPS-cell-derived mDA cells significantly protected grafted mDANs from needle-trauma-associated death and improved therapeutic outcomes in rodent models of Parkinson's disease with 6-hydroxydopamine lesions. Co-transplantation with T reg cells also suppressed the undesirable proliferation of TH - grafted cells, resulting in more compact grafts with a higher proportion and higher absolute numbers of TH + neurons. Together, these data emphasize the importance of the initial inflammatory response to surgical injury in the differential survival of cellular components of the graft, and suggest that co-transplanting autologous T reg cells effectively reduces the needle-trauma-induced death of mDANs, providing a potential strategy to achieve better clinical outcomes for cell therapy in Parkinson's disease.</snippet>
<snippet id="32474865">Title: Engraftable Induced Pluripotent Stem Cell-Derived Neural Precursors for Brain Repair.
Authors: Zygogianni, Ourania, Kouroupi, Georgia, Taoufik, Era et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: Methods in molecular biology (Clifton, N.J.)
Abstract: Stem cell transplantation has attracted great interest for treatment of neurodegenerative diseases to provide neuroprotection, repair the lesioned neuronal network and restore functionality. Parkinson's disease (PD), in particular, has been a preferred target because motor disability that constitutes a core pathology of the disease is associated with local loss of dopaminergic neurons in a specific brain area, the substantia nigra pars compacta. These cells project to the striatum where they deliver the neurotransmitter dopamine that is involved in control of many aspects of motor behavior. Therefore, cell transplantation approaches in PD aim to replenish dopamine deficiency in the striatum. A major challenge in developing cell therapy approaches is the ability to generate large numbers of transplantable cells in a reliable and reproducible manner. In recent years the technological breakthrough of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) has demonstrated that this is possible at a preclinical level, accelerating clinical translation. A second important issue is to efficiently differentiate iPSCs into dopaminergic neuronal progenitors with restricted proliferation potential in order to avoid cellular overgrowth in vivo and minimize the risk of tumorigenesis. Here we describe an effective protocol that includes human iPSC differentiation to the dopaminergic lineage and enrichment in neuronal precursor cells expressing the polysialylated form of the neural cell adhesion molecule PSA-NCAM, through magnetically activated cell sorting. The resulting cells are transplanted and shown to survive, differentiate, and integrate within a striatal lesion model generated by unilateral 6-hydroxydopamine administration in mice of the NOD/SCID strain that supports xenografts.</snippet>
<snippet id="36300203">Title: Therapeutic function of a novel rat induced pluripotent stem cell line in a 6‑OHDA‑induced rat model of Parkinson's disease.
Authors: Xu, Jiajia, Li, Yangyang, Zhu, Huan et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: International journal of molecular medicine
Abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative movement disorder of the central nervous system that results from the loss of dopaminergic (DA) nigral neurons. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) have shown potential for cell transplantation treatment of neurodegenerative disorders. In the present study, the small molecules CHIR99021 and RepSox (CR) significantly facilitated reprogramming and enhanced the efficiency of GFP+/iPS‑like colonies [rat iPSCs induced by OCT3/4, Sox2, Klf4, c‑Myc, Nanog and Lin28 + CR (RiPSCs‑6F/CR)] generation by ~4.0‑fold during lentivirus‑mediated reprogramming of six transcription factors in rat embryonic fibroblasts. The generation of iPSCs was detected by reverse transcription‑PCR, immunofluorescence and western blot analysis. Subsequently, RiPSCs‑6F/CR were stereotactically transplanted into the right medial forebrain bundle (MFB) of 6‑hydroxydopamine‑lesioned rats with PD. The transplanted RiPSCs‑6F/CR survived and functioned in the MFB of rats with PD for ≥20 weeks, and significantly improved functional restoration from their PD‑related behavioral defects. Furthermore, the grafted RiPSCs‑6F/CR could migrate and differentiate into various neurocytes in vivo, including γ aminobutyric acid‑ergic, DA neurons and glial cells. In conclusion, the present study confirmed that RiPSCs‑6F/CR induced by small molecules could be used as potential donor material for neural grafting to remodel basal ganglia circuitry in neurodegenerative diseases.</snippet>

Authors: Leitner, Dominique, Ramamoorthy, Mahesh, Dejosez, Marion et al. | Year: 2019 | Journal: Stem cell research
Abstract: Parkinson's disease is associated with the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the midbrain. Clinical studies investigating replacement of these neurons with in vitro-generated neurons are currently underway. Cryo-preservation may offer a solution, as it allows for banking of quality controlled mDA neurons. Authors: Tian, You-yong, Tang, Cui-Ju, Wang, Jia-ning et al. | Year: 2007 | Journal: Neuroscience letters
Abstract: Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) is a specific angiogenic peptide, which has been identified to play a critical role in neurodegeneration, and has beneficial effects on neurons. In this study, we investigated whether neurodegeneration in a rat model of Parkinson disease could be prevented by VEGF gene transfer mediated by adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors. Abstract: Vascular endothelial growth factor B (VEGF-B) has recently been shown to be a promising novel neuroprotective agent for several neurodegenerative conditions. Both doses of VEGF-B caused an increase in tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)-positive cell and fiber count in the substantia nigra (SN) and striatum in the neuroprotective experiment. The effect size was comparable to the effects seen with GDNF. In the neurorestoration paradigm, VEGF-B injection had no significant effect in either the behavioral or the immunohistochemical analyses, whereas GDNF injection significantly improved the amphetamine-induced rotational behavior and reduced TH-positive neuronal cell loss in the SN. <snippet id="19639608">Title: Reversible neurochemical changes mediated by delayed intrastriatal glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor gene delivery in a partial Parkinson's disease rat model.
Authors: Yang, Xin, Mertens, Birgit, Lehtonen, Enni et al. | Year: 2009 | Journal: The journal of gene medicine
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Efficient protection of dopaminergic neurons against a subsequent 6-hydroxydopamine lesion by glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) gene delivery has been demonstrated. By contrast, the neurorestorative effects of GDNF administered several weeks after the toxin have been less characterized. In particular, whether these were permanent or dependent on the continuous presence of GDNF remains elusive.

A tetracycline-inducible adeno-associated virus (AAV)-1 vector expressing human GDNF cDNA was administered unilaterally in the rat striatum 5 weeks after 6-hydroxydopamine. The amounts of tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), serine-40-phosphorylated TH (S40-TH) and aromatic amino acid decarboxylase (AADC) proteins were compared by western blotting and the dopamine levels quantified by high-performance liquid chromatography.

Dox-dependent behavioral improvements were demonstrated 4 weeks post-vector injection. data.title: Pre-clinical study of induced pluripotent stem cell-derived dopaminergic progenitor cells for Parkinson's disease.
data.abstract: Induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived dopaminergic (DA) neurons are an expected source for cell-based therapies for Parkinson's disease (PD). The regulatory criteria for the clinical application of these therapies, however, have not been established. Here we show the results of our pre-clinical study, in which we evaluate the safety and efficacy of dopaminergic progenitors (DAPs) derived from a clinical-grade human iPSC line. We confirm the characteristics of DAPs by in vitro analyses. We also verify that the DAP population include no residual undifferentiated iPSCs or early neural stem cells and have no genetic aberration in cancer-related genes. Furthermore, in vivo studies using immunodeficient mice reveal no tumorigenicity or toxicity of the cells. When the DAPs are transplanted into the striatum of 6-OHDA-lesioned rats, the animals show behavioral improvement. Based on these results, we started a clinical trial to treat PD patients in 2018.

data.title: Co-transplantation of autologous T reg cells in a cell therapy for Parkinson's disease.
data.abstract: The specific loss of midbrain dopamine neurons (mDANs) causes major motor dysfunction in Parkinson's disease, which makes cell replacement a promising therapeutic approach 1-4 . However, poor survival of grafted mDANs remains an obstacle to successful clinical outcomes 5-8 . Here we show that the surgical procedure itself (referred to here as 'needle trauma') triggers a profound host response that is characterized by acute neuroinflammation, robust infiltration of peripheral immune cells and brain cell death. When midbrain dopamine (mDA) cells derived from human induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells were transplanted into the rodent striatum, less than 10% of implanted tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) + mDANs survived at two weeks after transplantation. By contrast, TH - grafted cells mostly survived. Notably, transplantation of autologous regulatory T (T reg ) cells greatly modified the response to needle trauma, suppressing acute neuroinflammation and immune cell infiltration. Furthermore, intra-striatal co-transplantation of T reg cells and human-iPS-cell-derived mDA cells significantly protected grafted mDANs from needle-trauma-associated death and improved therapeutic outcomes in rodent models of Parkinson's disease with 6-hydroxydopamine lesions. Co-transplantation with T reg cells also suppressed the undesirable proliferation of TH - grafted cells, resulting in more compact grafts with a higher proportion and higher absolute numbers of TH + neurons. Together, these data emphasize the importance of the initial inflammatory response to surgical injury in the differential survival of cellular components of the graft, and suggest that co-transplanting autologous T reg cells effectively reduces the needle-trauma-induced death of mDANs, providing a potential strategy to achieve better clinical outcomes for cell therapy in Parkinson's disease.

data.title: Engraftable Induced Pluripotent Stem Cell-Derived Neural Precursors for Brain Repair.
data.abstract: Stem cell transplantation has attracted great interest for treatment of neurodegenerative diseases to provide neuroprotection, repair the lesioned neuronal network and restore functionality. Parkinson's disease (PD), in particular, has been a preferred target because motor disability that constitutes a core pathology of the disease is associated with local loss of dopaminergic neurons in a specific brain area, the substantia nigra pars compacta. These cells project to the striatum where they deliver the neurotransmitter dopamine that is involved in control of many aspects of motor behavior. Therefore, cell transplantation approaches in PD aim to replenish dopamine deficiency in the striatum. A major challenge in developing cell therapy approaches is the ability to generate large numbers of transplantable cells in a reliable and reproducible manner. In recent years the technological breakthrough of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) has demonstrated that this is possible at a preclinical level, accelerating clinical translation. A second important issue is to efficiently differentiate iPSCs into dopaminergic neuronal progenitors with restricted proliferation potential in order to avoid cellular overgrowth in vivo and minimize the risk of tumorigenesis. Here we describe an effective protocol that includes human iPSC differentiation to the dopaminergic lineage and enrichment in neuronal precursor cells expressing the polysialylated form of the neural cell adhesion molecule PSA-NCAM, through magnetically activated cell sorting. The resulting cells are transplanted and shown to survive, differentiate, and integrate within a striatal lesion model generated by unilateral 6-hydroxydopamine administration in mice of the NOD/SCID strain that supports xenografts.

data.title: Therapeutic function of a novel rat induced pluripotent stem cell line in a 6‑OHDA‑induced rat model of Parkinson's disease.
data.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative movement disorder of the central nervous system that results from the loss of dopaminergic (DA) nigral neurons. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) have shown potential for cell transplantation treatment of neurodegenerative disorders. In the present study, the small molecules CHIR99021 and RepSox (CR) significantly facilitated reprogramming and enhanced the efficiency of GFP+/iPS‑like colonies [rat iPSCs induced by OCT3/4, Sox2, Klf4, c‑Myc, Nanog and Lin28 + CR (RiPSCs‑6F/CR)] generation by ~4.0‑fold during lentivirus‑mediated reprogramming of six transcription factors in rat embryonic fibroblasts. The generation of iPSCs was detected by reverse transcription‑PCR, immunofluorescence and western blot analysis. Subsequently, RiPSCs‑6F/CR were stereotactically transplanted into the right medial forebrain bundle (MFB) of 6‑hydroxydopamine‑lesioned rats with PD. The transplanted RiPSCs‑6F/CR survived and functioned in the MFB of rats with PD for ≥20 weeks, and significantly improved functional restoration from their PD‑related behavioral defects. Furthermore, the grafted RiPSCs‑6F/CR could migrate and differentiate into various neurocytes in vivo, including γ aminobutyric acid‑ergic, DA neurons and glial cells. In conclusion, the present study confirmed that RiPSCs‑6F/CR induced by small molecules could be used as potential donor material for neural grafting to remodel basal ganglia circuitry in neurodegenerative diseases.

data.title: Immature mDA neurons ameliorate motor deficits in a 6-OHDA Parkinson's disease mouse model and are functional after cryopreservation.
data.abstract: Parkinson's disease is associated with the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the midbrain. Clinical studies investigating replacement of these neurons with in vitro-generated neurons are currently underway. However, this approach has been limited by difficulties in scaling up on-demand production of midbrain dopaminergic (mDA) neurons from pluripotent stem cells. Cryo-preservation may offer a solution, as it allows for banking of quality controlled mDA neurons. In this study, we tested different freezing conditions and found that optimal cryopreservation of immature human mDA neurons at an early differentiation time point was achieved in STEM-CELLBANKER medium using a controlled freezing program.

# Overview

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is characterized by motor neuron degeneration and the presence of cytoplasmic, ubiquitinated TDP-43 inclusions in affected neurons. TDP-43 is an RNA/DNA-binding protein whose aberrant cytoplasmic accumulation, hyperphosphorylation, and ubiquitination are central to ALS pathogenesis, occurring in both familial and sporadic disease and even preceding clinical onset in many patients. Below, we synthesize proposed pathogenic mechanisms by which TDP-43 aggregation contributes to motor neuron degeneration and summarize therapeutic strategies that target TDP-43 pathology, highlighting preclinical and early clinical evidence.

# Proposed Pathogenic Mechanisms of TDP-43 Aggregation in ALS

1. **Gain-of-toxic-function from mislocalized and post-translationally modified TDP-43**  
   Pathogenic TARDBP mutations and environmental or genetic modifiers promote cytoplasmic mislocalization of TDP-43 and alter its post-translational modifications (e.g., phosphorylation, ubiquitination), converting normally nuclear RNA-binding activity into cytoplasmic toxicity. These modifications favor aggregation and inclusion formation, which are hallmark features in ALS spinal cord and brainstem motor neurons. The majority of sporadic ALS cases show TDP-43 inclusions, underscoring its centrality to disease pathobiology.

2. **Amyloid-like fibrillization and oligomer toxicity**  
   In vitro, hyperphosphorylated and ubiquitinated TDP-43 exhibits amyloid-like aggregation tendencies. While physiological phase-separated condensates are normal cellular structures, pathological oligomerization and fibrillization are implicated in neuronal injury. Toxic oligomers may disrupt RNA metabolism, sequester essential proteins, and impair cellular functions critical for motor neuron survival.

3. **Disruption of RNA metabolism and splicing**  
   TDP-43 is a key regulator of RNA processing, including alternative splicing, transport, and stability. Cytoplasmic accumulation and aggregation of TDP-43 perturb these processes, leading to aberrant RNA/protein products that can trigger stress responses, endoplasmic reticulum and proteostasis dysfunction, and ultimately cell death.

4. **Cytoskeletal and axonal transport defects**  
   TDP-43 interacts with cytoskeletal components (e.g., neurofilaments, microtubules, and actin regulators), including via regulation of mRNAs for cytoskeletal proteins. TDP-43 aggregation correlates with reduced axon formation and length, and with elevated cytoskeletal biomarkers (e.g., phosphorylated neurofilament heavy chain, NFL), reflecting impaired axonal transport and structural integrity—key contributors to motor neuron degeneration.

5. **Prion-like propagation and spread**  
   TDP-43 pathology shows features reminiscent of prion-like spread: templated misfolding/propagation along neural circuits, regional vulnerability, and liquid–liquid phase separation that can seed further aggregation. This mechanism could explain the regional and temporal pattern of motor neuron involvement and disease progression.

6. **Mitochondrial and endocytic/mitophagic dysfunction**  
   TDP-43 aggregation has been linked to mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired endocytic pathways, contributing to energy failure and apoptotic or necroptotic cell death. These processes, combined with proteostasis stress from aggregation, exacerbate motor neuron vulnerability.

7. **Upstream triggers in wild-type TDP-43**  
   Since most ALS cases lack TARDBP mutations, upstream events—such as stress, aging, or interactions with other proteins (e.g., FUS) that perturb RNA metabolism—may drive pathological transitions in wild-type TDP-43, promoting aggregation and downstream toxicity.

# Therapeutic Strategies Targeting TDP-43 Pathology

1. **TDP-43 Degradation and Disaggregation Approaches**  
   Small molecules and chaperones aimed at reducing TDP-43 stability or reversing aberrant post-translational modifications (e.g., dephosphorylation, deubiquitination) have shown promise in preclinical models by lowering cytoplasmic TDP-43 levels and reducing aggregate burden, thereby improving neuronal survival and function. Reviews highlight emerging strategies toward TDP-43 disaggregation and ALS therapeutics, though most remain at early experimental stages.

2. **RNA-Targeted Therapies Modulating TDP-43-Dependent Pathways**  
   Because TDP-43 regulates RNA metabolism, antisense and other RNA-targeted strategies aim to normalize aberrant splicing or expression of cytoskeletal and transport genes driven by TDP-43 dysregulation. Preclinical studies indicate that restoring proper RNA processing can mitigate aggregation-related toxicity and axonal defects.

3. **Targeting Cytoskeletal Consequences of TDP-43 Aggregation**  
   Therapies that stabilize or repair cytoskeletal networks (e.g., microtubules, neurofilaments) or enhance axonal transport may indirectly counteract TDP-43–driven degeneration by addressing downstream effects of TDP-43 mislocalization. Biomarkers like pNFH and NFL, which correlate with TDP-43 pathology, are used clinically to track disease severity and may guide stratification in targeted trials.

4. **Anti-Aggregation and Anti-Prion-Like Propagation Strategies**  
   Compounds that disrupt phase separation or inhibit templated aggregation/seed propagation of TDP-43 inclusions are under investigation. These approaches aim to break the cycle of regional spread and chronic proteostasis stress that characterizes ALS.

5. **Combination with Disease-Modifying ALS Treatments**  
   Approved ALS therapies (e.g., riluzole, edaravone) provide modest survival benefit and are being integrated with strategies that address TDP-43 pathology. Antisense oligonucleotides (e.g., tofersen targeting SOD1) illustrate the feasibility of CNS-targeted RNA therapies; while tofersen targets FUS in clinical use, the pipeline underscores that RNA/protein-targeted strategies can reduce toxic protein burden and may be combined with TDP-43–directed approaches in future trials.

# Evidence Status and Gaps

- Strong mechanistic and translational evidence supports TDP-43 as a central driver of ALS pathology, with robust human pathological data and convergence across genetic and cellular models.  
- Preclinical studies demonstrate that lowering or disrupting TDP-43 pathology can ameliorate motor neuron dysfunction, axonal degeneration, and survival in animal models and cellular systems.  
- Early clinical efforts focused on other ALS proteins (e.g., SOD1, FUS) via antisense oligonucleotides and other modalities, establishing feasibility for CNS delivery and protein reduction; however, direct, TDP-43–targeted small molecules or biologics remain largely preclinical, and combination regimens targeting multiple TDP-43 mechanisms are an active area of development.  
- Key gaps include definitive human evidence that clearing TDP-43 aggregates improves clinical outcomes, and optimization of strategies that distinguish toxic oligomers from physiological functions to avoid off-target effects on essential RNA metabolism.

# Conclusion

TDP-43 aggregation contributes to ALS through multiple convergent mechanisms: mislocalization and post-translational modification, amyloid-like fibrillization and oligomer toxicity, disruption of RNA metabolism, cytoskeletal and axonal transport failure, and prion-like spread, with additional contributions from mitochondrial and endocytic/mitophagic dysfunction. Therapeutic strategies targeting TDP-43 pathology span degradation/disaggregation, RNA-targeted modulation, cytoskeletal support, and anti-propagation approaches, with preclinical efficacy and emerging early clinical precedents for CNS-targeted RNA therapies that reduce toxic protein burdens. Continued refinement of TDP-43–specific agents and biomarker-guided clinical trials are needed to translate these mechanisms into durable disease modification.

While the majority of ALS cases (90-95%) are sporadic (sALS), among familial ALS cases 5-10% involve the inheritance of mutations in the TARDBP gene and the remaining (90-95%) are due to mutations in other genes such as: C9ORF72, SOD1, FUS , and NEK1 etc. Strikingly however, the majority of sporadic ALS patients (up to 97%) also contain the TDP-43 protein deposited in the neuronal inclusions, which suggests of its pivotal role in the ALS pathology. Thus, unraveling the molecular mechanisms of the TDP-43 pathology seems central to the ALS therapeutics, hence, we comprehensively review the current understanding of the TDP-43's pathology in ALS. We discuss the roles of TDP-43's mutations, its cytoplasmic mis-localization and aberrant post-translational modifications in ALS. Also, we evaluate TDP-43's amyloid-like in vitro aggregation, its physiological vs. pathological oligomerization in vivo , liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), and potential prion-like propagation propensity of the TDP-43 inclusions. Finally, we describe the various evolving TDP-43-induced toxicity mechanisms, such as the impairment of endocytosis and mitotoxicity etc. and also discuss the emerging strategies toward TDP-43 disaggregation and ALS therapeutics.

trajectory.final_answer:
# Overview

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is characterized by motor neuron degeneration and the presence of cytoplasmic, ubiquitinated TDP-43 inclusions in affected neurons. TDP-43 is an RNA/DNA-binding protein whose aberrant cytoplasmic accumulation, hyperphosphorylation, and ubiquitination are central to ALS pathogenesis, occurring in both familial and sporadic disease and even preceding clinical onset in many patients. Below, we synthesize proposed pathogenic mechanisms by which TDP-43 aggregation contributes to motor neuron degeneration and summarize therapeutic strategies that target TDP-43 pathology, highlighting preclinical and early clinical evidence.

# Proposed Pathogenic Mechanisms of TDP-43 Aggregation in ALS

1. **Gain-of-toxic-function from mislocalized and post-translationally modified TDP-43**  
   Pathogenic TARDBP mutations and environmental or genetic modifiers promote cytoplasmic mislocalization of TDP-43 and alter its post-translational modifications (e.g., phosphorylation, ubiquitination), converting normally nuclear RNA-binding activity into cytoplasmic toxicity. These modifications favor aggregation and inclusion formation, which are hallmark features in ALS spinal cord and brainstem motor neurons. The majority of sporadic ALS cases show TDP-43 inclusions, underscoring its centrality to disease pathobiology.

2. **Amyloid-like fibrillization and oligomer toxicity**  
   In vitro, hyperphosphorylated and ubiquitinated TDP-43 exhibits amyloid-like aggregation tendencies. While physiological phase-separated condensates are normal cellular structures, pathological oligomerization and fibrillization are implicated in neuronal injury. Toxic oligomers may disrupt RNA metabolism, sequester essential proteins, and impair cellular functions critical for motor neuron survival.

3. **Disruption of RNA metabolism and splicing**  
   TDP-43 is a key regulator of RNA processing, including alternative splicing, transport, and stability. Cytoplasmic accumulation and aggregation of TDP-43 perturb these processes, leading to aberrant RNA/protein products that can trigger stress responses, endoplasmic reticulum and proteostasis dysfunction, and ultimately cell death.

4. **Cytoskeletal and axonal transport defects**  
   TDP-43 interacts with cytoskeletal components (e.g., neurofilaments, microtubules, and actin regulators), including via regulation of mRNAs for cytoskeletal proteins. TDP-43 aggregation correlates with reduced axon formation and length, and with elevated cytoskeletal biomarkers (e.g., phosphorylated neurofilament heavy chain, NFL), reflecting impaired axonal transport and structural integrity—key contributors to motor neuron degeneration.

5. **Prion-like propagation and spread**  
   TDP-43 pathology shows features reminiscent of prion-like spread: templated misfolding/propagation along neural circuits, regional vulnerability, and liquid–liquid phase separation that can seed further aggregation. This mechanism could explain the regional and temporal pattern of motor neuron involvement and disease progression.

6. **Mitochondrial and endocytic/mitophagic dysfunction**  
   TDP-43 aggregation has been linked to mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired endocytic pathways, contributing to energy failure and apoptotic or necroptotic cell death. These processes, combined with proteostasis stress from aggregation, exacerbate motor neuron vulnerability.

7. **Upstream triggers in wild-type TDP-43**  
   Since most ALS cases lack TARDBP mutations, upstream events—such as stress, aging, or interactions with other proteins (e.g., FUS) that perturb RNA metabolism—may drive pathological transitions in wild-type TDP-43, promoting aggregation and downstream toxicity.

# Therapeutic Strategies Targeting TDP-43 Pathology

1. **TDP-43 Degradation and Disaggregation Approaches**  
   Small molecules and chaperones aimed at reducing TDP-43 stability or reversing aberrant post-translational modifications (e.g., dephosphorylation, deubiquitination) have shown promise in preclinical models by lowering cytoplasmic TDP-43 levels and reducing aggregate burden, thereby improving neuronal survival and function. Reviews highlight emerging strategies toward TDP-43 disaggregation and ALS therapeutics, though most remain at early experimental stages.

2. **RNA-Targeted Therapies Modulating TDP-43-Dependent Pathways**  
   Because TDP-43 regulates RNA metabolism, antisense and other RNA-targeted strategies aim to normalize aberrant splicing or expression of cytoskeletal and transport genes driven by TDP-43 dysregulation. Preclinical studies indicate that restoring proper RNA processing can mitigate aggregation-related toxicity and axonal defects.

3. **Targeting Cytoskeletal Consequences of TDP-43 Aggregation**  
   Therapies that stabilize or repair cytoskeletal networks (e.g., microtubules, neurofilaments) or enhance axonal transport may indirectly counteract TDP-43–driven degeneration by addressing downstream effects of TDP-43 mislocalization. Biomarkers like pNFH and NFL, which correlate with TDP-43 pathology, are used clinically to track disease severity and may guide stratification in targeted trials.

4. **Anti-Aggregation and Anti-Prion-Like Propagation Strategies**  
   Compounds that disrupt phase separation or inhibit templated aggregation/seed propagation of TDP-43 inclusions are under investigation. These approaches aim to break the cycle of regional spread and chronic proteostasis stress that characterizes ALS.

5. **Combination with Disease-Modifying ALS Treatments**  
   Approved ALS therapies (e.g., riluzole, edaravone) provide modest survival benefit and are being integrated with strategies that address TDP-43 pathology. Antisense oligonucleotides (e.g., tofersen targeting SOD1) illustrate the feasibility of CNS-targeted RNA therapies; while tofersen targets FUS in clinical use, the pipeline underscores that RNA/protein-targeted strategies can reduce toxic protein burden and may be combined with TDP-43–directed approaches in future trials.

# Evidence Status and Gaps

- Strong mechanistic and translational evidence supports TDP-43 as a central driver of ALS pathology, with robust human pathological data and convergence across genetic and cellular models.  
- Preclinical studies demonstrate that lowering or disrupting TDP-43 pathology can ameliorate motor neuron dysfunction, axonal degeneration, and survival in animal models and cellular systems.  
- Early clinical efforts focused on other ALS proteins (e.g., SOD1, FUS) via antisense oligonucleotides and other modalities, establishing feasibility for CNS delivery and protein reduction; however, direct, TDP-43–targeted small molecules or biologics remain largely preclinical, and combination regimens targeting multiple TDP-43 mechanisms are an active area of development.  
- Key gaps include definitive human evidence that clearing TDP-43 aggregates improves clinical outcomes, and optimization of strategies that distinguish toxic oligomers from physiological functions to avoid off-target effects on essential RNA metabolism.

# Conclusion

TDP-43 aggregation contributes to ALS through multiple convergent mechanisms: mislocalization and post-translational modification, amyloid-like fibrillization and oligomer toxicity, disruption of RNA metabolism, cytoskeletal and axonal transport failure, and prion-like spread, with additional contributions from mitochondrial and endocytic/mitophagic dysfunction. Therapeutic strategies targeting TDP-43 pathology span degradation/disaggregation, RNA-targeted modulation, cytoskeletal support, and anti-propagation approaches, with preclinical efficacy and emerging early clinical precedents for CNS-targeted RNA therapies that reduce toxic protein burdens. Continued refinement of TDP-43–specific agents and biomarker-guided clinical trials are needed to translate these mechanisms into durable disease modification.
