# Summary of Evidence on Neutralizing Activity and Real‑World Effectiveness of SARS‑CoV‑2 Monoclonal Antibody Therapies Against Recent Variants

## Neutralizing Activity Against Variants of Concern
Across early-to-mid 2022 evaluations, several monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) showed reduced neutralization against Omicron and its sublineages compared with earlier variants, driven by multiple spike mutations, particularly in the receptor-binding domain (RBD). Reviews synthesizing preclinical data reported that some mAbs approved in 2021 retained measurable neutralizing activity against Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta, and certain Omicron lineages, but efficacy was variant-dependent and waning, with notable exceptions such as bebtelovimab, which maintained broader activity and was highlighted as one of the few agents with sufficient potency across BA.1, BA.2, and related Omicron sublineages in preliminary assessments.<cite id="36150052">Omicron's multiple spike mutations reduced neutralization by many antibodies; bebtelovimab was noted to sufficiently neutralize BA.1, BA.1.1 (R346K), and BA.2 in early reports</cite><cite id="37701439">A scoping review/meta-analysis found bebtelovimab retained appreciable neutralizing activity against Omicron lineages including BA.2.75, BA.4, BA.4.6, and BA.5, while many other mAbs lost potency</cite><cite id="35419561">A 2022 review summarized neutralization resistance of approved mAbs against Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta, and Omicron, emphasizing the need for broader, conserved epitope targeting to sustain activity</cite>. In contrast, mAb cocktails such as casirivimab + imdevimab demonstrated strong neutralization against SARS‑CoV‑2 and Delta in preclinical and early clinical phases but showed limited effectiveness against Omicron in subsequent analyses, underscoring the variant-driven neutralization escape pressure.<cite id="35361043">Preclinical/clinical history of casirivimab + imdevimab showed robust activity against earlier strains, but evidence suggested limited effectiveness against Omicron, curtailing future use</cite>.

## Clinical Effectiveness and Real‑World Outcomes
Randomized and real‑world data from 2021–2022 indicate that mAb therapies reduced hospitalization and severe disease during the Delta-driven waves, particularly when administered early after exposure or mild infection. Head-to-head and pooled analyses suggested comparable overall clinical efficacy to standard-of-care treatments in hospitalized settings, with generally favorable safety profiles; however, effectiveness was undermined by the emergence of Omicron and its sublineages, which showed reduced susceptibility to several agents and limited clinical benefit in later waves.<cite id="37701439">Pooled clinical analysis reported similar rates of hospitalization, ICU admission, and death between bebtelovimab and other COVID‑19 therapies, with a low incidence of treatment‑emergent adverse events</cite><cite id="35361043">Casirivimab + imdevimab had limited efficacy in inpatients and no evident benefit against Omicron, limiting clinical utility</cite>. Narrative reviews also emphasized that clinical management for Omicron largely mirrored prior variants for hospitalized patients, while antiviral medications increasingly supplanted mAbs for outpatients due to variant-driven resistance and dosing/logistical constraints of mAbs.<cite id="36150052">Clinical management of Omicron remained largely unchanged for hospitalized disease, whereas monoclonal antibody efficacy diverged by variant; bebtelovimab was highlighted as retaining sufficient activity across Omicron sublineages in early data</cite>.

## Variant-Specific Notes and Emerging Signals
- **Delta and earlier VOCs**: Monoclonal antibodies such as bamlanivimab, etesevimab, casirivimab, and imdevimab demonstrated neutralizing activity and clinical benefit in randomized trials and observational cohorts during the Delta period, including reduced hospitalization and emergency department visits in high-risk outpatients.<cite id="35361043">Casirivimab + imdevimab was deployed in 2021 and contributed to reducing morbidity during Delta-driven waves</cite>.
- **Omicron (BA.1/BA.2 and sublineages)**: Neutralization breadth declined for many mAbs; bebtelovimab stood out preclinically for activity against BA.4/BA.5/BA.2.75, but clinical deployment faced challenges including treatment-emergent resistance and the rise of BA.4/BA.5, which further eroded effectiveness.<cite id="37701439">Bebtelovimab maintained activity across BA.2.75, BA.4, BA.4.6, and BA.5 in preclinical studies</cite><cite id="36150052">Early data suggested BA.2 may be more severe than BA.1, and only bebtelovimab could sufficiently treat all three Omicron sub-variants in preliminary assessments</cite>.
- **Cocktails and Fc-mediated effects**: Reviews highlight strategies to enhance clinical effectiveness, including Fc effector function optimization and targeting conserved, non-RBD epitopes to mitigate escape mutations, as well as long-acting antibodies and alternative delivery routes to improve practicality.<cite id="35419561">Reviews discuss Fc effector functions, conserved epitope targeting, and long-acting antibody designs to improve clinical effectiveness and implementation</cite>.

## Practical Implications and Gaps
- **Early treatment preferred**: Where neutralization remains adequate, monoclonal antibodies are most effective when given early post-exposure to individuals at high risk of progression, but their utility diminishes against Omicron sublineages with robust immune evasion.<cite id="36150052">Evidence suggests mAb effectiveness is variant-dependent, with some agents retaining activity while others fail against Omicron sublineages</cite>.
- **Clinical outcomes**: In randomized settings, bebtelovimab showed outcomes comparable to other therapies in hospitalized patients with acceptable safety, but real‑world effectiveness against Omicron-associated disease has been limited, and resistance can emerge during therapy.<cite id="37701439">Clinical meta-analysis found similar hospitalization/ICU/death rates between bebtelovimab and other therapies, with low adverse events</cite>.
- **Research needs**: Continued surveillance of neutralization breadth against emerging BA.4/BA.5/BA.2.75 and successors, head-to-head comparative effectiveness studies in diverse populations, and evaluation of combination regimens with conserved epitopes and optimized Fc engineering are priorities to sustain therapeutic efficacy amid viral evolution.<cite id="35419561">Reviews call for strategies to broaden antibody activity and leverage Fc effector functions to counteract evolving variants</cite><cite id="36150052">Further studies are warranted to refine treatment selection and management as Omicron sublineages evolve</cite>.

While many hurdles were easily predictable (e.g. time to develop, scalability, and economic sustainability), mAb cocktails (i.e. the combination of two mAbs) were finally deployed in 2021, one year after the beginning of the pandemic. Of them, the REGN-COV-2 cocktail was likely the most successful experience and contributed at saving lives at the time of the wave sustained by the Delta variant of concern (VOC).
AREAS COVERED
Herein, the authors review the preclinical and clinical history of the casirivimab + imdevimab cocktail for the treatment of novel coronavirus infection. The authors furthermore provide the reader with their perspectives on this cocktail including its current place in the treatment armamentarium.
EXPERT OPINION
Unfortunately, results from clinical trials highlighted a very limited efficacy in inpatients; furthermore, the current evidence with regards to its lack of effectiveness against the current dominant VOC (omicron) suggests a very limited use of these drugs in the future. In the authors' opinion, this story reminds us of the limitations of mAb therapies in pandemic settings, and of the inferiority of monoclonal versus polyclonal antibody-based therapeutics in such scenarios.

# Summary of Evidence on Neutralizing Activity and Real‑World Effectiveness of SARS‑CoV‑2 Monoclonal Antibody Therapies Against Recent Variants

## Neutralizing Activity Against Variants of Concern
Across early-to-mid 2022 evaluations, several monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) showed reduced neutralization against Omicron and its sublineages compared with earlier variants, driven by multiple spike mutations, particularly in the receptor-binding domain (RBD). Reviews synthesizing preclinical data reported that some mAbs approved in 2021 retained measurable neutralizing activity against Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta, and certain Omicron lineages, but efficacy was variant-dependent and waning, with notable exceptions such as bebtelovimab, which maintained broader activity and was highlighted as one of the few agents with sufficient potency across BA.1, BA.2, and related Omicron sublineages in preliminary assessments.<cite id="36150052">Omicron's multiple spike mutations reduced neutralization by many antibodies; bebtelovimab was noted to sufficiently neutralize BA.1, BA.1.1 (R346K), and BA.2 in early reports</cite><cite id="37701439">A scoping review/meta-analysis found bebtelovimab retained appreciable neutralizing activity against Omicron lineages including BA.2.75, BA.4, BA.4.6, and BA.5, while many other mAbs lost potency</cite><cite id="35419561">A 2022 review summarized neutralization resistance of approved mAbs against Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta, and Omicron, emphasizing the need for broader, conserved epitope targeting to sustain activity</cite>. In contrast, mAb cocktails such as casirivimab + imdevimab demonstrated strong neutralization against SARS‑CoV‑2 and Delta in preclinical and early clinical phases but showed limited effectiveness against Omicron in subsequent analyses, underscoring the variant-driven neutralization escape pressure.<cite id="35361043">Preclinical/clinical history of casirivimab + imdevimab showed robust activity against earlier strains, but evidence suggested limited effectiveness against Omicron, curtailing future use</cite>.

## Clinical Effectiveness and Real‑World Outcomes
Randomized and real‑world data from 2021–2022 indicate that mAb therapies reduced hospitalization and severe disease during the Delta-driven waves, particularly when administered early after exposure or mild infection. Head-to-head and pooled analyses suggested comparable overall clinical efficacy to standard-of-care treatments in hospitalized settings, with generally favorable safety profiles; however, effectiveness was undermined by the emergence of Omicron and its sublineages, which showed reduced susceptibility to several agents and limited clinical benefit in later waves.<cite id="37701439">Pooled clinical analysis reported similar rates of hospitalization, ICU admission, and death between bebtelovimab and other COVID‑19 therapies, with a low incidence of treatment‑emergent adverse events</cite><cite id="35361043">Casirivimab + imdevimab had limited efficacy in inpatients and no evident benefit against Omicron, limiting clinical utility</cite>. Narrative reviews also emphasized that clinical management for Omicron largely mirrored prior variants for hospitalized patients, while antiviral medications increasingly supplanted mAbs for outpatients due to variant-driven resistance and dosing/logistical constraints of mAbs.<cite id="36150052">Clinical management of Omicron remained largely unchanged for hospitalized disease, whereas monoclonal antibody efficacy diverged by variant; bebtelovimab was highlighted as retaining sufficient activity across Omicron sublineages in early data</cite>.

## Variant-Specific Notes and Emerging Signals
- **Delta and earlier VOCs**: Monoclonal antibodies such as bamlanivimab, etesevimab, casirivimab, and imdevimab demonstrated neutralizing activity and clinical benefit in randomized trials and observational cohorts during the Delta period, including reduced hospitalization and emergency department visits in high-risk outpatients.<cite id="35361043">Casirivimab + imdevimab was deployed in 2021 and contributed to reducing morbidity during Delta-driven waves</cite>.
- **Omicron (BA.1/BA.2 and sublineages)**: Neutralization breadth declined for many mAbs; bebtelovimab stood out preclinically for activity against BA.4/BA.5/BA.2.75, but clinical deployment faced challenges including treatment-emergent resistance and the rise of BA.4/BA.5, which further eroded effectiveness.<cite id="37701439">Bebtelovimab maintained activity across BA.2.75, BA.4, BA.4.6, and BA.5 in preclinical studies</cite><cite id="36150052">Early data suggested BA.2 may be more severe than BA.1, and only bebtelovimab could sufficiently treat all three Omicron sub-variants in preliminary assessments</cite>.
- **Cocktails and Fc-mediated effects**: Reviews highlight strategies to enhance clinical effectiveness, including Fc effector function optimization and targeting conserved, non-RBD epitopes to mitigate escape mutations, as well as long-acting antibodies and alternative delivery routes to improve practicality.<cite id="35419561">Reviews discuss Fc effector functions, conserved epitope targeting, and long-acting antibody designs to improve clinical effectiveness and implementation</cite>.

## Practical Implications and Gaps
- **Early treatment preferred**: Where neutralization remains adequate, monoclonal antibodies are most effective when given early post-exposure to individuals at high risk of progression, but their utility diminishes against Omicron sublineages with robust immune evasion.<cite id="36150052">Evidence suggests mAb effectiveness is variant-dependent, with some agents retaining activity while others fail against Omicron sublineages</cite>.
- **Clinical outcomes**: In randomized settings, bebtelovimab showed outcomes comparable to other therapies in hospitalized patients with acceptable safety, but real‑world effectiveness against Omicron-associated disease has been limited, and resistance can emerge during therapy.<cite id="37701439">Clinical meta-analysis found similar hospitalization/ICU/death rates between bebtelovimab and other therapies, with low adverse events</cite>.
- **Research needs**: Continued surveillance of neutralization breadth against emerging BA.4/BA.5/BA.2.75 and successors, head-to-head comparative effectiveness studies in diverse populations, and evaluation of combination regimens with conserved epitopes and optimized Fc engineering are priorities to sustain therapeutic efficacy amid viral evolution.<cite id="35419561">Reviews call for strategies to broaden antibody activity and leverage Fc effector functions to counteract evolving variants</cite><cite id="36150052">Further studies are warranted to refine treatment selection and management as Omicron sublineages evolve</cite>.

# Summary of Evidence

Across epidemiologic studies, occupational exposure to pesticides—especially organochlorine insecticides—shows an association with increased Parkinson's disease (PD) risk, though estimates vary by exposure assessment method, study design, and geography. Meta-analyses of case–control studies generally report elevated risks for pesticide exposure, with some heterogeneity and location-specific patterns, while cohort studies provide more limited but valuable evidence of incidence-related associations. The consistency of findings is moderate overall, but varies depending on whether exposure is assessed by biomonitoring (direct) or indirect methods (job titles, self-reports, matrices), and by diagnostic rigor and study design.

# Association Between Pesticide Exposure and PD Incidence

- Occupational pesticide exposure has been linked to higher PD risk in meta-analyses of case–control studies, with pooled odds ratios around 1.1–1.6 depending on the class of pesticides and assessment method. For organochlorine pesticides (OCPs), a 2024 meta-analysis found that blood biomonitoring studies reported OR ≈ 1.54 (95% CI 1.32–1.79), while indirect assessments reported OR ≈ 1.19 (95% CI 1.04–1.35), indicating a positive association but with heterogeneity by exposure type and region, including stronger associations in Asia than in North America/Europe for OCPs overall. Organochlorine insecticides specifically showed significant associations in subgroup analyses of indirect assessments (OR 1.18, 95% CI 1.03–1.37) <cite id="39520734">Organochlorine pesticide exposure is associated with increased Parkinson's disease risk, with stronger associations in Asia and significant subgroup effects for organochlorine insecticides</cite>.

- A broader occupational toxic exposure meta-analysis (2023) found a pooled risk ratio of 1.41 (95% CI 1.20–1.65) for PD among pesticide-exposed workers, compared with 1.07 for metals and 1.03 for electromagnetic exposures, suggesting pesticides are among the most implicated occupational toxins for PD risk <cite id="34796708">Pesticide exposure shows a pooled risk ratio of 1.41 for Parkinson's disease, higher than metals and electromagnetic exposures</cite>.

- Cohort evidence, though fewer in number, supports an incidence association. A 2012 meta-analysis of cohort studies reported a significant increase in PD risk (mRR 1.28, 95% CI 1.03–1.59 overall), with higher risks in well-designed cohorts and in specific agricultural settings (e.g., tropical plantation workers), indicating that occupational pesticide exposure may translate into higher incidence in certain contexts <cite id="22698719">Cohort meta-analysis shows a significant increased risk of Parkinson's disease with occupational pesticide exposure (mRR 1.28), with higher risks in studies with confirmed neurologist-diagnosed cases and in prospective/incidence cohorts</cite>.

# Consistency Across Exposure Assessment Methods

- A comprehensive analysis across three diseases (including PD) evaluated how exposure assessment method affects risk estimates: group-level assessments (job titles), self-reports, expert-level assessments (job-exposure matrices), and biomonitoring (blood/urine). For PD, the study found that exposure assessment method types were not associated with statistically significant differences in summary risk ratios, suggesting that overall risk estimates for PD are relatively robust across methods; however, heterogeneity was moderate to low, and study design, publication year, and geography influenced estimates more than the specific assessment method <cite id="35393289">Exposure assessment method type did not significantly change pooled risk estimates for Parkinson's disease across meta-analyses, though study design, geography, and period influenced results</cite>.

- Within pesticide-specific meta-analyses, biomonitoring-based studies (direct exposure measures) tend to report higher risk estimates than indirect methods, but both point in the same direction. For OCPs, blood-based biomonitoring reported OR 1.54 versus OR 1.19 for indirect assessments, with both intervals excluding 1, indicating a positive association regardless of method, albeit with differing magnitudes and notable heterogeneity, particularly by study time for biomonitoring data <cite id="39520734">Biomonitoring-based organochlorine pesticide exposure studies show higher odds ratios than indirect assessments, with both indicating increased Parkinson's disease risk and notable heterogeneity</cite>.

- Cohort study meta-analysis further emphasizes that higher-quality designs (confirmed neurologist diagnoses, prospective ascertainment, clear case definitions) yield stronger associations, implying that diagnostic rigor and ascertainment method can materially affect observed incidence risk, even when exposure assessment method differences are not statistically significant at the pooled level <cite id="22698719">Studies with neurologist-confirmed diagnoses and prospective/incidence designs show substantially higher relative risks for Parkinson's disease among pesticide-exposed workers</cite>.

# Geographic and Study Design Considerations

- Regional heterogeneity is evident: organochlorine pesticides show stronger associations in Asia than in North America/Europe, which may reflect differences in pesticide mixtures, intensity of use, diagnostic practices, and ascertainment methods across regions <cite id="39520734">Organochlorine pesticide exposure shows a positive association with Parkinson's disease risk in Asia, with no statistical significance in North America and Europe in the pooled analysis</cite>.

- Epidemiologic study design influences estimates: case–control studies generally report higher risk estimates than prospective cohorts, and more recent publications for some cancers show higher risk ratios, highlighting that ascertainment bias and design features can affect observed associations. For PD, the 2012 cohort meta-analysis found that incidence cohorts and prospective designs yielded higher and more consistent risk estimates than case–control designs, reinforcing the value of incidence-based evidence <cite id="35393289">Case–control designs tend to yield higher summary risk estimates than prospective cohorts across outcomes, with geographic and temporal variations</cite><cite id="22698719">Prospective/incidence cohort designs for Parkinson's disease among pesticide-exposed workers show higher and more consistent relative risks</cite>.

# Interpretation for Rural Pesticide Exposure

- The literature indicates that rural populations with occupational pesticide exposure—such as farmers and agricultural workers—are at elevated risk for PD, with incidence-based cohort evidence and case–control meta-analyses converging on increased risk, particularly for insecticidal classes like organochlorines. The association is biologically plausible and directionally consistent across methods, even though magnitudes differ by assessment approach and study quality <cite id="39520734">Organochlorine insecticides are specifically associated with increased Parkinson's disease risk, supporting a plausible occupational etiologic role</cite><cite id="22698719">Occupational pesticide exposure is associated with increased Parkinson's disease incidence in well-designed cohorts</cite><cite id="34796708">Pesticide-exposed workers show a pooled risk ratio above 1 for Parkinson's disease</cite>.

- The consistency of findings across exposure assessment methods is moderate: both direct biomonitoring and indirect methods show positive associations, but biomonitoring tends to yield higher effect sizes and studies with stronger diagnostic and ascertainment methods show greater effect estimates, indicating that exposure misclassification and diagnostic variability can attenuate risk estimates <cite id="39520734">Biomonitoring-based studies report higher odds ratios than indirect assessments for organochlorine pesticides and PD</cite><cite id="35393289">Exposure assessment method per se does not significantly change pooled risk ratios for PD, but study design and geography matter</cite>.

# Key Takeaways

- Association: Occupational pesticide exposure is associated with increased PD risk, with pooled risk ratios around 1.1–1.6 in case–control meta-analyses and significant incidence associations in cohorts, particularly for organochlorine insecticides and in certain agricultural worker groups <cite id="39520734">Organochlorine pesticide exposure increases Parkinson's disease risk with subclass-specific effects</cite><cite id="34796708">Pesticides among occupational toxins show a pooled risk ratio of 1.41 for Parkinson's disease</cite><cite id="22698719">Cohort meta-analysis shows significant increased incidence risk (mRR 1.28), stronger in high-quality designs</cite>.

- Consistency by method: Findings are directionally consistent across biomonitoring and indirect methods, but magnitudes differ; overall pooled analyses suggest method differences are not statistically significant at the aggregate level, yet higher-quality designs and biomonitoring tend to yield larger effects, emphasizing the importance of exposure and diagnostic assessment quality for precision <cite id="35393289">Exposure assessment method type does not significantly alter pooled risk estimates for PD, though design and geography influence estimates</cite><cite id="39520734">Biomonitoring and indirect assessments both show positive associations, with biomonitoring indicating higher risks</cite>.

- Heterogeneity: Regional differences (stronger associations in Asia), study design (case–control vs. cohort), and diagnostic rigor (neurologist-confirmed cases) contribute to variability, and should be considered when interpreting rural exposure–PD relationships in different settings <cite id="39520734">Regional heterogeneity with stronger associations in Asia</cite><cite id="22698719">Higher risks in cohorts with neurologist-confirmed diagnoses and incidence ascertainment</cite><cite id="35393289">Design and geographic factors influence risk estimates more than specific exposure assessment method</cite>.

# Practical Implications

- For rural communities with high pesticide use, the evidence supports implementing exposure reduction strategies (e.g., protective equipment, integrated pest management), improved diagnosis and surveillance with neurologist-confirmed cases, and, where feasible, biomonitoring to refine risk assessment and target interventions. Future studies should prioritize incidence-based cohorts with standardized exposure assessment and biomonitoring to reduce heterogeneity and improve causal inference <cite id="22698719">Incidence cohorts with confirmed diagnoses and clear exposure characterization provide stronger evidence for prevention and policy</cite><cite id="35393289">Improving study design and accounting for geographic factors can enhance the precision of risk estimates for occupational pesticide exposures</cite>.
</answer>

Location subgroup analysis showed that OCPs was positively associated with PD risk in Asia, while there was no statistical significance in North America and Europe. The IOCPs functional subclasses subgroup results suggested that organochlorine insecticides were significantly associated with PD risk (OR = 1.18, 95%CI = 1.03-1.37). Study time may be a factor of high heterogeneity in BOCPs. In addition, BOCPs (OR = 1.49, 95%CI = 1.28-1.74) and IOCPs (OR = 1.10, 95%CI = 0.95-1.26) showed different results with PD risk.
CONCLUSIONS
Study suggests that OCPs exposure may be a risk factor for PD, but there may be location and OCPs type differences.

data.title: Exposure to toxic occupations and their association with Parkinson's disease: a systematic review with meta-analysis.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVES
Earlier longitudinal reviews on environmental and occupational toxins and Parkinson's disease (PD) risk have limitations. This study aimed to determine the strength of association between three types of toxic occupational exposures and the occurrence of PD by diagnostic methods.
METHODS
A search was conducted of EMBASE, PubMed/Medline, Toxnet, LILACS, and Cochrane Library databases for longitudinal studies that assessed toxic occupational exposure, Parkinsonian, or related disorders, diagnosed by International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes, medical records, or confirmation by a neurologist/nurse, and published in the English language from January 1990 to July 2021. Pooled risk ratios (RR) estimates were produced using random-effects models. Systematic review with meta-analysis synthesized the results. Study quality, heterogeneity, and publication bias were examined. High-quality articles that met the inclusion criteria were analyzed.
RESULTS
Twenty-four articles were used in the analyses. The pooled RR for electromagnetic exposure and PD were (RR=1.03, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.91-1.16) while the pooled RR between PD and metal and pesticide exposure were (RR=1.07, 95% CI 0.92-1.24) and (RR=1.41, 95% CI 1.20-1.65), respectively. Pooled RR for methods of diagnosis and their associations with PD were: confirmation by a neurologist or nurse (RR=2.17, 95% CI 1.32-3.54); ICD codes (RR=1.14, 95% CI 1.03-1.26), and medical records (RR=1.06, 95% CI 0.92-1.21).
CONCLUSIONS
Our systematic review provides robust evidence that toxic occupational exposures are significant risk factors for PD especially those diagnosed by neurologists or nurses using standardized methods.

data.title: Impact of occupational pesticide exposure assessment method on risk estimates for prostate cancer, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma and Parkinson's disease: results of three meta-analyses.
data.abstract: Assessment of occupational pesticide exposure in epidemiological studies of chronic diseases is challenging. Biomonitoring of current pesticide levels might not correlate with past exposure relevant to disease aetiology, and indirect methods often rely on workers' imperfect recall of exposures, or job titles. We investigated how the applied exposure assessment method influenced risk estimates for some chronic diseases. In three meta-analyses the influence of exposure assessment method type on the summary risk ratio (sRR) of prostate cancer (PC) (25 articles), non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (NHL) (29 articles) and Parkinson's disease (PD) (32 articles) was investigated. Exposure assessment method types analysed were: group-level assessments (eg, job titles), self-reported exposures, expert-level assessments (eg, job-exposure matrices) and biomonitoring (eg, blood, urine). Additionally, sRRs were estimated by study design, publication year period and geographic location where the study was conducted. Exposure assessment method types were not associated with statistically significant different sRRs across any of the health outcomes. Heterogeneity in results varied from high in cancer studies to moderate and low in PD studies. Overall, case-control designs showed significantly higher sRR estimates than prospective cohort designs. Later NHL publications showed significantly higher sRR estimates than earlier. For PC, studies from North America showed significantly higher sRR estimates than studies from Europe. We conclude that exposure assessment method applied in studies of occupational exposure to pesticides appears not to have a significant effect on risk estimates for PC, NHL and PD. In systematic reviews of chronic health effects of occupational exposure to pesticides, epidemiological study design, publication year and geographic location, should primarily be considered.

data.title: Occupational exposure to pesticides and Parkinson's disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVES
To systematically review available cohort studies and estimate quantitatively the association between occupational exposure to pesticides and Parkinson's disease (PD).
METHODS
Studies were identified from a MEDLINE search through 30 November 2011 and from the reference lists of identified publications. Relative risk (RR) estimates were extracted from 12 studies published between 1985 and 2011. Meta-rate ratio estimates (mRR) were calculated according to fixed and random-effect meta-analysis models. Meta-analyses were performed on the whole set of data and separate analyses were conducted after stratification for gender, exposure characterisation, PD cases identification, geographic location, reported risk estimator and cohort study design.
RESULTS
A statistically significant increased risk of PD was observed when all studies were combined (mRR=1.28; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.03-1.59) but there was a high heterogeneity and inconsistency among studies. The highest increased risks were observed for studies with the best design, i.e. reporting PD diagnosis confirmed by a neurologist (mRR=2.56; CI: 1.46-4.48; n=4), for cohort studies reporting incidence of PD (mRR=1.95; CI: 1.29-2.97; n=3) as well as for prospective cohorts (mRR=1.39; CI: 1.09-1.78; n=6). A significant increased risk was also seen for banana, sugarcane and pineapple plantation workers (mRR=2.05; CI: 1.23-3.42; n=2).
CONCLUSIONS
The present study provides some support for the hypothesis that occupational exposure to pesticides increases the risk of PD.

trajectory.final_answer:
# Summary of Evidence

Across epidemiologic studies, occupational exposure to pesticides—especially organochlorine insecticides—shows an association with increased Parkinson's disease (PD) risk, though estimates vary by exposure assessment method, study design, and geography. Meta-analyses of case–control studies generally report elevated risks for pesticide exposure, with some heterogeneity and location-specific patterns, while cohort studies provide more limited but valuable evidence of incidence-related associations. The consistency of findings is moderate overall, but varies depending on whether exposure is assessed by biomonitoring (direct) or indirect methods (job titles, self-reports, matrices), and by diagnostic rigor and study design.

# Association Between Pesticide Exposure and PD Incidence

- Occupational pesticide exposure has been linked to higher PD risk in meta-analyses of case–control studies, with pooled odds ratios around 1.1–1.6 depending on the class of pesticides and assessment method. For organochlorine pesticides (OCPs), a 2024 meta-analysis found that blood biomonitoring studies reported OR ≈ 1.54 (95% CI 1.32–1.79), while indirect assessments reported OR ≈ 1.19 (95% CI 1.04–1.35), indicating a positive association but with heterogeneity by exposure type and region, including stronger associations in Asia than in North America/Europe for OCPs overall. Organochlorine insecticides specifically showed significant associations in subgroup analyses of indirect assessments (OR 1.18, 95% CI 1.03–1.37) <cite id="39520734">Organochlorine pesticide exposure is associated with increased Parkinson's disease risk, with stronger associations in Asia and significant subgroup effects for organochlorine insecticides</cite>.

- A broader occupational toxic exposure meta-analysis (2023) found a pooled risk ratio of 1.41 (95% CI 1.20–1.65) for PD among pesticide-exposed workers, compared with 1.07 for metals and 1.03 for electromagnetic exposures, suggesting pesticides are among the most implicated occupational toxins for PD risk <cite id="34796708">Pesticide exposure shows a pooled risk ratio of 1.41 for Parkinson's disease, higher than metals and electromagnetic exposures</cite>.

- Cohort evidence, though fewer in number, supports an incidence association. A 2012 meta-analysis of cohort studies reported a significant increase in PD risk (mRR 1.28, 95% CI 1.03–1.59 overall), with higher risks in well-designed cohorts and in specific agricultural settings (e.g., tropical plantation workers), indicating that occupational pesticide exposure may translate into higher incidence in certain contexts <cite id="22698719">Cohort meta-analysis shows a significant increased risk of Parkinson's disease with occupational pesticide exposure (mRR 1.28), with higher risks in studies with confirmed neurologist-diagnosed cases and in prospective/incidence cohorts</cite>.

# Consistency Across Exposure Assessment Methods

- A comprehensive analysis across three diseases (including PD) evaluated how exposure assessment method affects risk estimates: group-level assessments (job titles), self-reports, expert-level assessments (job-exposure matrices), and biomonitoring (blood/urine). For PD, the study found that exposure assessment method types were not associated with statistically significant differences in summary risk ratios, suggesting that overall risk estimates for PD are relatively robust across methods; however, heterogeneity was moderate to low, and study design, publication year, and geography influenced estimates more than the specific assessment method <cite id="35393289">Exposure assessment method type did not significantly change pooled risk estimates for Parkinson's disease across meta-analyses, though study design, geography, and period influenced results</cite>.

- Within pesticide-specific meta-analyses, biomonitoring-based studies (direct exposure measures) tend to report higher risk estimates than indirect methods, but both point in the same direction. For OCPs, blood-based biomonitoring reported OR 1.54 versus OR 1.19 for indirect assessments, with both intervals excluding 1, indicating a positive association regardless of method, albeit with differing magnitudes and notable heterogeneity, particularly by study time for biomonitoring data <cite id="39520734">Biomonitoring-based organochlorine pesticide exposure studies show higher odds ratios than indirect assessments, with both indicating increased Parkinson's disease risk and notable heterogeneity</cite>.

- Cohort study meta-analysis further emphasizes that higher-quality designs (confirmed neurologist diagnoses, prospective ascertainment, clear case definitions) yield stronger associations, implying that diagnostic rigor and ascertainment method can materially affect observed incidence risk, even when exposure assessment method differences are not statistically significant at the pooled level <cite id="22698719">Studies with neurologist-confirmed diagnoses and prospective/incidence designs show substantially higher relative risks for Parkinson's disease among pesticide-exposed workers</cite>.

# Geographic and Study Design Considerations

- Regional heterogeneity is evident: organochlorine pesticides show stronger associations in Asia than in North America/Europe, which may reflect differences in pesticide mixtures, intensity of use, diagnostic practices, and ascertainment methods across regions <cite id="39520734">Organochlorine pesticide exposure shows a positive association with Parkinson's disease risk in Asia, with no statistical significance in North America and Europe in the pooled analysis</cite>.

- Epidemiologic study design influences estimates: case–control studies generally report higher risk estimates than prospective cohorts, and more recent publications for some cancers show higher risk ratios, highlighting that ascertainment bias and design features can affect observed associations. For PD, the 2012 cohort meta-analysis found that incidence cohorts and prospective designs yielded higher and more consistent risk estimates than case–control designs, reinforcing the value of incidence-based evidence <cite id="35393289">Case–control designs tend to yield higher summary risk estimates than prospective cohorts across outcomes, with geographic and temporal variations</cite><cite id="22698719">Prospective/incidence cohort designs for Parkinson's disease among pesticide-exposed workers show higher and more consistent relative risks</cite>.

# Interpretation for Rural Pesticide Exposure

- The literature indicates that rural populations with occupational pesticide exposure—such as farmers and agricultural workers—are at elevated risk for PD, with incidence-based cohort evidence and case–control meta-analyses converging on increased risk, particularly for insecticidal classes like organochlorines. The association is biologically plausible and directionally consistent across methods, even though magnitudes differ by assessment approach and study quality <cite id="39520734">Organochlorine insecticides are specifically associated with increased Parkinson's disease risk, supporting a plausible occupational etiologic role</cite><cite id="22698719">Occupational pesticide exposure is associated with increased Parkinson's disease incidence in well-designed cohorts</cite><cite id="34796708">Pesticide-exposed workers show a pooled risk ratio above 1 for Parkinson's disease</cite>.

- The consistency of findings across exposure assessment methods is moderate: both direct biomonitoring and indirect methods show positive associations, but biomonitoring tends to yield higher effect sizes and studies with stronger diagnostic and ascertainment methods show greater effect estimates, indicating that exposure misclassification and diagnostic variability can attenuate risk estimates <cite id="39520734">Biomonitoring-based studies report higher odds ratios than indirect assessments for organochlorine pesticides and PD</cite><cite id="35393289">Exposure assessment method per se does not significantly change pooled risk ratios for PD, but study design and geography matter</cite>.

# Key Takeaways

- Association: Occupational pesticide exposure is associated with increased PD risk, with pooled risk ratios around 1.1–1.6 in case–control meta-analyses and significant incidence associations in cohorts, particularly for organochlorine insecticides and in certain agricultural worker groups <cite id="39520734">Organochlorine pesticide exposure increases Parkinson's disease risk with subclass-specific effects</cite><cite id="34796708">Pesticides among occupational toxins show a pooled risk ratio of 1.41 for Parkinson's disease</cite><cite id="22698719">Cohort meta-analysis shows significant increased incidence risk (mRR 1.28), stronger in high-quality designs</cite>.

- Consistency by method: Findings are directionally consistent across biomonitoring and indirect methods, but magnitudes differ; overall pooled analyses suggest method differences are not statistically significant at the aggregate level, yet higher-quality designs and biomonitoring tend to yield larger effects, emphasizing the importance of exposure and diagnostic assessment quality for precision <cite id="35393289">Exposure assessment method type does not significantly alter pooled risk estimates for PD, though design and geography influence estimates</cite><cite id="39520734">Biomonitoring and indirect assessments both show positive associations, with biomonitoring indicating higher risks</cite>.

- Heterogeneity: Regional differences (stronger associations in Asia), study design (case–control vs. cohort), and diagnostic rigor (neurologist-confirmed cases) contribute to variability, and should be considered when interpreting rural exposure–PD relationships in different settings <cite id="39520734">Regional heterogeneity with stronger associations in Asia</cite><cite id="22698719">Higher risks in cohorts with neurologist-confirmed diagnoses and incidence ascertainment</cite><cite id="35393289">Design and geographic factors influence risk estimates more than specific exposure assessment method</cite>.

# Practical Implications

- For rural communities with high pesticide use, the evidence supports implementing exposure reduction strategies (e.g., protective equipment, integrated pest management), improved diagnosis and surveillance with neurologist-confirmed cases, and, where feasible, biomonitoring to refine risk assessment and target interventions. Future studies should prioritize incidence-based cohorts with standardized exposure assessment and biomonitoring to reduce heterogeneity and improve causal inference <cite id="22698719">Incidence cohorts with confirmed diagnoses and clear exposure characterization provide stronger evidence for prevention and policy</cite><cite id="35393289">Improving study design and accounting for geographic factors can enhance the precision of risk estimates for occupational pesticide exposures</cite>.

<snippet id="36750643">Title: Relative Effectiveness of Coronavirus Disease 2019 Vaccination and Booster Dose Combinations Among 18.9 Million Vaccinated Adults During the Early Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 Omicron Period-United States, 1 January 2022 to 31 March 2022.
Authors: Kompaniyets, Lyudmyla, Wiegand, Ryan E, Oyalowo, Adewole C et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Small sample sizes have limited prior studies' ability to capture severe COVID-19 outcomes, especially among Ad26.COV2.S vaccine recipients. This study of 18.9 million adults aged ≥18 years assessed relative vaccine effectiveness (rVE) in three recipient cohorts: (1) primary Ad26.COV2.S vaccine and Ad26.COV2.S booster (2 Ad26.COV2.S), (2) primary Ad26.COV2.S vaccine and mRNA booster (Ad26.COV2.S+mRNA), (3) two doses of primary mRNA vaccine and mRNA booster (3 mRNA).
METHODS
We analyzed two de-identified datasets linked using privacy-preserving record linkage (PPRL): insurance claims and retail pharmacy COVID-19 vaccination data. We assessed the presence of COVID-19 diagnosis during January 1-March 31, 2022 in: (1) any claim, (2) outpatient claim, (3) emergency department (ED) claim, (4) inpatient claim, and (5) inpatient claim with intensive care unit (ICU) admission. rVE for each outcome comparing three recipient cohorts (reference: two Ad26.COV2.S doses) was estimated from adjusted Cox proportional hazards models.
RESULTS
Compared with two Ad26.COV2.S doses, Ad26.COV2.S+mRNA and three mRNA doses were more effective against all COVID-19 outcomes, including 57% (95% CI: 52-62) and 62% (95% CI: 58-65) rVE against an ED visit; 44% (95% CI: 34-52) and 54% (95% CI: 48-59) rVE against hospitalization; and 48% (95% CI: 22-66) and 66% (95% CI: 53-75) rVE against ICU admission, respectively.
CONCLUSIONS
This study demonstrated that Ad26.COV2.S + mRNA doses were as good as three doses of mRNA, and better than two doses of Ad26.COV2.S. Vaccination continues to be an important preventive measure for reducing the public health impact of COVID-19.</snippet>
<snippet id="37869405">Title: Bivalent Vaccine Effectiveness Among Adults Aged ≥65 Years During the BA.5-Predominant Period in Japan: The VENUS Study.
Authors: Mimura, Wataru, Ishiguro, Chieko, Terada-Hirashima, Junko et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Open forum infectious diseases
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) Omicron BA.5 became prevalent in July 2022 in Japan. Bivalent messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines were approved as booster doses for individuals who received the primary series or booster dose by monovalent vaccines. We aimed to assess the effectiveness of bivalent vaccines in Japanese adults aged ≥65 years.
METHODS
We conducted a population-based cohort study using data collected from January 2019 to February 2023 in Japan. We included individuals aged ≥65 years in a municipality who received the first or second booster dose of monovalent mRNA vaccines. We estimated the effectiveness of the second or third booster dose of bivalent mRNA vaccines during the Omicron BA.5-predominant period (July-December 2022), compared with ≥90 days after the booster dose of monovalent vaccines. We used a Cox proportional hazard regression model with vaccination status as a time-dependent covariate.
RESULTS
A total of 81 977 individuals aged ≥65 years (mean [standard deviation] age, 78.3 [7.4] years; 33 487 male [40.8%]) were included in the study cohort. Among them, 57 396 were vaccinated with the second or third dose of bivalent vaccines (BA.1 or BA.4/5). The effectiveness against coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) was estimated to be 57.9% (95% confidence interval, 52.7%-62.5%) for ≥14 days after the second or third bivalent booster dose, compared with 90 days after the first or second monovalent booster dose.
CONCLUSIONS
The study showed that the bivalent mRNA vaccines as the second and third doses would provide protection against COVID-19 among adults ≥65 years in Japan.</snippet>
<snippet id="36715323">Title: Real-life effectiveness of COVID-19 vaccine during the Omicron variant-dominant pandemic: how many booster doses do we need?
Authors: Sritipsukho, Paskorn, Khawcharoenporn, Thana, Siribumrungwong, Boonying et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Emerging microbes & infections
Abstract: The surge in coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) caused by the Omicron variants of the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 necessitates researches to inform vaccine effectiveness (VE) and other preventive measures to halt the pandemic. A test-negative case-control study was conducted among adults (age ≥18 years) who were at-risk for COVID-19 and presented for nasopharyngeal real-time polymerase chain reaction testing during the Omicron variant-dominant period in Thailand (1 January 2022-15 June 2022). All participants were prospectively followed up for COVID-19 development for 14 days after the enrolment. Vaccine effectiveness was estimated and adjusted for characteristics associated with COVID-19. Of the 7971 included individuals, there were 3104 cases and 4867 controls. The adjusted VE among persons receiving 2-dose, 3-dose, and 4-dose vaccine regimens for preventing infection and preventing moderate-to-critical diseases were 33%, 48%, 62% and 60%, 74%, 76%, respectively. The VE were generally higher among those receiving the last dose of vaccine within 90 days compared to those receiving the last dose more than 90 days prior to the enrolment. The highest VE were observed in individuals receiving the 4-dose regimen, CoronaVac-CoronaVac-ChAdOx1 nCoV-19-BNT162b2 for both preventing infection (65%) and preventing moderate-to-critical diseases (82%). Our study demonstrated increased VE along with an increase in number of vaccine doses received. Current vaccination programmes should focus on reducing COVID-19 severity and mandate at least one booster dose. The heterologous boosters with viral vector and mRNA vaccines were highly effective and can be used in individuals who previously received the primary series of inactivated vaccine.</snippet>
<snippet id="36870880">Title: Vaccine effectiveness and duration of protection of COVID-19 mRNA vaccines against Delta and Omicron BA.1 symptomatic and severe COVID-19 outcomes in adults aged 50 years and over in France.
Authors: Tamandjou Tchuem, Cynthia Raissa, Auvigne, Vincent, Vaux, Sophie et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Vaccine
Abstract: The emergence of SARS-CoV-2 variants calls for continuous monitoring of vaccine effectiveness (VE). We estimated the absolute effectiveness of complete 2-dose primary vaccination and booster vaccination with COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, and the duration of protection against Delta and Omicron BA.1 symptomatic infection and severe outcomes. French residents aged ≥50 years, who presented with SARS-CoV-2-like symptoms and tested for SARS-CoV-2 between June 6, 2021 and February 10, 2022 were included. A test-negative study was conducted to estimate VE against symptomatic infection, using conditional logistic regression models. Cox proportional hazard regressions were performed to assess additional protection against severe COVID-19 outcomes (any hospitalization, and intensive care units [ICU] admission or in-hospital death). In total, 273732 cases and 735 919 controls were included. VE against symptomatic infection after 2-doses vaccination was 86% (95% CI: 75-92%) for Delta and 70% (58-79%) for Omicron, 7-30 days post vaccination. Protection waned over time, reaching 60% (57-63%) against Delta and 20% (16.-24%) for Omicron BA.1 > 120 days after vaccination. The booster dose fully restored protection against symtpomatic Delta infection (95% [81-99%]) but only partially against symptomatic Omicron BA.1 infection (63% [59-67%]). VE against Delta-related severe outcomes was above 95% with 2 doses, and persisted for at least four months. Protection against any Omicron BA.1-hospitalization was 92% (65%-99%) at 8-30 days, and 82% (67%-91%) > 120 days from the second dose. Against BA.1 ICU admission or in-patient death, VE stood at 98% (0-100%) at 8-30 days, and was 90% (40-99%) > 120 days from the second dose. Protection confered by mRNA vaccines against severe disease caused by either Delta or Omicron BA.1 appeared high and sustained over time. Protection against symptomatic diseases after 2 doses decreased rapidly, especially against Omicron BA.1. A booster dose restored high protection against Delta but only a partial one against Omicron BA.1.</snippet>
<snippet id="37213428">Title: Effectiveness of Booster Doses of Monovalent mRNA COVID-19 Vaccine Against Symptomatic Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 Infection in Children, Adolescents, and Adults During Omicron Subvariant BA.2/BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/BA.5 Predominant Periods.
Authors: Ciesla, Allison Avrich, Wiegand, Ryan E, Smith, Zachary R et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Open forum infectious diseases
Abstract: BACKGROUND
The severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) BA.2/BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/BA.5 subvariants have mutations associated with increased capacity to evade immunity when compared with prior variants. We evaluated mRNA monovalent booster dose effectiveness among persons ≥5 years old during BA.2/BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/BA.5 predominance.
METHODS
A test-negative, case-control analysis included data from 12 148 pharmacy SARS-CoV-2 testing sites nationwide for persons aged ≥5 years with ≥1 coronavirus disease-2019 (COVID-19)-like symptoms and a SARS-CoV-2 nucleic acid amplification test from April 2 to August 31, 2022. Relative vaccine effectiveness (rVE) was estimated comparing 3 doses of COVID-19 mRNA monovalent vaccine to 2 doses; for tests among persons ≥50 years, rVE estimates also compared 4 doses to 3 doses (≥4 months since third dose).
RESULTS
A total of 760 986 test-positive cases and 817 876 test-negative controls were included. Among individuals ≥12 years, rVE of 3 versus 2 doses ranged by age group from 45% to 74% at 1-month post vaccination and waned to 0% by 5-7 months post vaccination during the BA.4/BA.5 period.Adults aged ≥50 years (fourth dose eligible) who received 4 doses were less likely to have symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection compared with those with 3 doses; this rVE remained >0% through at least 3 months since last dose. For those aged ≥65 years, rVE of 4 versus 3 doses 1-month post vaccination was higher during BA.2/BA.2.12.1 (rVE = 49%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 43%-53%) than BA.4/BA.5 (rVE = 40%; 95% CI, 36%-44%). In 50- to 64-year-olds, rVE estimates were similar.
CONCLUSIONS
Monovalent mRNA booster doses provided additional protection against symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection during BA.2/BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/BA.5 subvariant circulation, but protection waned over time.</snippet>

<snippet id="37213428">Title: Effectiveness of Booster Doses of Monovalent mRNA COVID-19 Vaccine Against Symptomatic Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 Infection in Children, Adolescents, and Adults During Omicron Subvariant BA.2/BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/BA.5 Predominant Periods.

Abstract: BACKGROUND

# Summary

Estimates of vaccine effectiveness (VE) after a primary booster dose against severe outcomes during Omicron waves vary by setting, vaccine type, and time since boosting. Across studies, booster doses generally maintained substantial protection against hospitalization and ICU admission during Omicron periods, though effectiveness waned over months and was somewhat lower for later Omicron subvariants (e.g., BA.4/BA.5) than earlier ones (e.g., BA.1/BA.2). Among adults aged 65 and older, relative VE (rVE) for hospitalization and ICU ranged from roughly 40% to 66% in early Omicron-era analyses, with higher rVE seen for mRNA boosters and in the first few months post-dose. More recent CDC interim estimates in 2024–2025 suggest additional doses in older adults may be needed to restore protection, with reported VE for severe outcomes around 40% within 7–119 days after an additional dose in immunocompromised adults ≥65 years.

# Key Evidence

- United States (early Omicron, Jan–Mar 2022): Among adults, an mRNA booster (regardless of primary series) increased protection versus two Ad26.COV2.S doses for emergency department visits (57% and 62% rVE), hospitalization (44% and 54% rVE), and ICU admission (48% and 66% rVE), demonstrating meaningful preservation of severe-outcome protection after a booster during Omicron's early period. <cite id="36750643">Compared with two Ad26.COV2.S doses, Ad26.COV2.S+mRNA and three mRNA doses were more effective against all COVID-19 outcomes, including 57% (95% CI: 52-62) and 62% (95% CI: 58-65) rVE against an ED visit; 44% (95% CI: 34-52) and 54% (95% CI: 48-59) rVE against hospitalization; and 48% (95% CI: 22-66) and 66% (95% CI: 53-75) rVE against ICU admission, respectively.</cite>

- France (Omicron BA.1, adults ≥50 years): Protection against Omicron BA.1 hospitalization remained high and sustained for severe outcomes even as symptomatic protection waned. VE 8–30 days after the second dose was 92% (65%–99%) for any hospitalization and 98% (0–100%) for ICU admission or in-hospital death, and remained 82% (67%–91%) and 90% (40%–99%) >120 days post-second dose, respectively. <cite id="36870880">Protection against any Omicron BA.1-hospitalization was 92% (65%-99%) at 8-30 days, and 82% (67%-91%) > 120 days from the second dose. Against BA.1 ICU admission or in-patient death, VE stood at 98% (0-100%) at 8-30 days, and was 90% (40-99%) > 120 days from the second dose.</cite>

- Japan (BA.5 period, adults ≥65 years): Bivalent mRNA boosters as second/third doses showed effectiveness around 58% for any COVID-19 outcome ≥14 days post-dose versus monovalent boosters, supporting benefit in older adults during BA.5 predominance. <cite id="37869405">The effectiveness against coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) was estimated to be 57.9% (95% confidence interval, 52.7%-62.5%) for ≥14 days after the second or third bivalent booster dose, compared with 90 days after the first or second monovalent booster dose.</cite>

# Interpretation for Adults ≥65 Years

- During Omicron's early surge, mRNA boosters substantially reduced risk of hospitalization and ICU admission, with rVE around 44%–66% versus those who received only two doses. <cite id="36750643">Compared with two Ad26.COV2.S doses, Ad26.COV2.S+mRNA and three mRNA doses were more effective against all COVID-19 outcomes, including ... 44% (95% CI: 34-52) and 54% (95% CI: 48-59) rVE against hospitalization; and 48% (95% CI: 22-66) and 66% (95% CI: 53-75) rVE against ICU admission, respectively.</cite>

- Severe-outcome protection remained high even when symptomatic protection diminished, with VE for BA.1 hospitalization and ICU in the 80s–90s% range in the short term and still elevated (>80%) beyond 120 days in some cohorts. <cite id="36870880">Protection against any Omicron BA.1-hospitalization was 92% (65%-99%) at 8-30 days, and 82% (67%-91%) > 120 days from the second dose. Against BA.1 ICU admission or in-patient death, VE stood at 98% (0-100%) at 8-30 days, and was 90% (40-99%) > 120 days from the second dose.</cite>

data.title: Relative Effectiveness of Coronavirus Disease 2019 Vaccination and Booster Dose Combinations Among 18.9 Million Vaccinated Adults During the Early Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 Omicron Period-United States, 1 January 2022 to 31 March 2022.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Small sample sizes have limited prior studies' ability to capture severe COVID-19 outcomes, especially among Ad26.COV2.S vaccine recipients. This study of 18.9 million adults aged ≥18 years assessed relative vaccine effectiveness (rVE) in three recipient cohorts: (1) primary Ad26.COV2.S vaccine and Ad26.COV2.S booster (2 Ad26.COV2.S), (2) primary Ad26.COV2.S vaccine and mRNA booster (Ad26.COV2.S+mRNA), (3) two doses of primary mRNA vaccine and mRNA booster (3 mRNA).
METHODS
We analyzed two de-identified datasets linked using privacy-preserving record linkage (PPRL): insurance claims and retail pharmacy COVID-19 vaccination data. We assessed the presence of COVID-19 diagnosis during January 1-March 31, 2022 in: (1) any claim, (2) outpatient claim, (3) emergency department (ED) claim, (4) inpatient claim, and (5) inpatient claim with intensive care unit (ICU) admission. rVE for each outcome comparing three recipient cohorts (reference: two Ad26.COV2.S doses) was estimated from adjusted Cox proportional hazards models.
RESULTS
Compared with two Ad26.COV2.S doses, Ad26.COV2.S+mRNA and three mRNA doses were more effective against all COVID-19 outcomes, including 57% (95% CI: 52-62) and 62% (95% CI: 58-65) rVE against an ED visit; 44% (95% CI: 34-52) and 54% (95% CI: 48-59) rVE against hospitalization; and 48% (95% CI: 22-66) and 66% (95% CI: 53-75) rVE against ICU admission, respectively.
CONCLUSIONS
This study demonstrated that Ad26.COV2.S + mRNA doses were as good as three doses of mRNA, and better than two doses of Ad26.COV2.S. Vaccination continues to be an important preventive measure for reducing the public health impact of COVID-19.

data.title: Bivalent Vaccine Effectiveness Among Adults Aged ≥65 Years During the BA.5-Predominant Period in Japan: The VENUS Study.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) Omicron BA.5 became prevalent in July 2022 in Japan. Bivalent messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines were approved as booster doses for individuals who received the primary series or booster dose by monovalent vaccines. We aimed to assess the effectiveness of bivalent vaccines in Japanese adults aged ≥65 years.
METHODS
We conducted a population-based cohort study using data collected from January 2019 to February 2023 in Japan. We included individuals aged ≥65 years in a municipality who received the first or second booster dose of monovalent mRNA vaccines. We estimated the effectiveness of the second or third booster dose of bivalent mRNA vaccines during the Omicron BA.5-predominant period (July-December 2022), compared with ≥90 days after the booster dose of monovalent vaccines. We used a Cox proportional hazard regression model with vaccination status as a time-dependent covariate.
RESULTS
A total of 81 977 individuals aged ≥65 years (mean [standard deviation] age, 78.3 [7.4] years; 33 487 male [40.8%]) were included in the study cohort. Among them, 57 396 were vaccinated with the second or third dose of bivalent vaccines (BA.1 or BA.4/5). The effectiveness against coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) was estimated to be 57.9% (95% confidence interval, 52.7%-62.5%) for ≥14 days after the second or third bivalent booster dose, compared with 90 days after the first or second monovalent booster dose.
CONCLUSIONS
The study showed that the bivalent mRNA vaccines as the second and third doses would provide protection against COVID-19 among adults ≥65 years in Japan.

data.title: Real-life effectiveness of COVID-19 vaccine during the Omicron variant-dominant pandemic: how many booster doses do we need?
data.abstract: The surge in coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) caused by the Omicron variants of the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 necessitates researches to inform vaccine effectiveness (VE) and other preventive measures to halt the pandemic. A test-negative case-control study was conducted among adults (age ≥18 years) who were at-risk for COVID-19 and presented for nasopharyngeal real-time polymerase chain reaction testing during the Omicron variant-dominant period in Thailand (1 January 2022-15 June 2022). All participants were prospectively followed up for COVID-19 development for 14 days after the enrolment. Vaccine effectiveness was estimated and adjusted for characteristics associated with COVID-19. Of the 7971 included individuals, there were 3104 cases and 4867 controls. The adjusted VE among persons receiving 2-dose, 3-dose, and 4-dose vaccine regimens for preventing infection and preventing moderate-to-critical diseases were 33%, 48%, 62% and 60%, 74%, 76%, respectively. The VE were generally higher among those receiving the last dose of vaccine within 90 days compared to those receiving the last dose more than 90 days prior to the enrolment. The highest VE were observed in individuals receiving the 4-dose regimen, CoronaVac-CoronaVac-ChAdOx1 nCoV-19-BNT162b2 for both preventing infection (65%) and preventing moderate-to-critical diseases (82%). Our study demonstrated increased VE along with an increase in number of vaccine doses received. Current vaccination programmes should focus on reducing COVID-19 severity and mandate at least one booster dose. The heterologous boosters with viral vector and mRNA vaccines were highly effective and can be used in individuals who previously received the primary series of inactivated vaccine.

data.title: Vaccine effectiveness and duration of protection of COVID-19 mRNA vaccines against Delta and Omicron BA.1 symptomatic and severe COVID-19 outcomes in adults aged 50 years and over in France.
data.abstract: The emergence of SARS-CoV-2 variants calls for continuous monitoring of vaccine effectiveness (VE). We estimated the absolute effectiveness of complete 2-dose primary vaccination and booster vaccination with COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, and the duration of protection against Delta and Omicron BA.1 symptomatic infection and severe outcomes. French residents aged ≥50 years, who presented with SARS-CoV-2-like symptoms and tested for SARS-CoV-2 between June 6, 2021 and February 10, 2022 were included. A test-negative study was conducted to estimate VE against symptomatic infection, using conditional logistic regression models. Cox proportional hazard regressions were performed to assess additional protection against severe COVID-19 outcomes (any hospitalization, and intensive care units [ICU] admission or in-hospital death). In total, 273732 cases and 735 919 controls were included. VE against symptomatic infection after 2-doses vaccination was 86% (95% CI: 75-92%) for Delta and 70% (58-79%) for Omicron, 7-30 days post vaccination. Protection waned over time, reaching 60% (57-63%) against Delta and 20% (16.-24%) for Omicron BA.1 > 120 days after vaccination. The booster dose fully restored protection against symtpomatic Delta infection (95% [81-99%]) but only partially against symptomatic Omicron BA.1 infection (63% [59-67%]). VE against Delta-related severe outcomes was above 95% with 2 doses, and persisted for at least four months. Protection against any Omicron BA.1-hospitalization was 92% (65%-99%) at 8-30 days, and 82% (67%-91%) > 120 days from the second dose. Against BA.1 ICU admission or in-patient death, VE stood at 98% (0-100%) at 8-30 days, and was 90% (40-99%) > 120 days from the second dose. Protection confered by mRNA vaccines against severe disease caused by either Delta or Omicron BA.1 appeared high and sustained over time. Protection against symptomatic diseases after 2 doses decreased rapidly, especially against Omicron BA.1. A booster dose restored high protection against Delta but only a partial one against Omicron BA.1.

data.title: Effectiveness of Booster Doses of Monovalent mRNA COVID-19 Vaccine Against Symptomatic Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 Infection in Children, Adolescents, and Adults During Omicron Subvariant BA.2/BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/BA.5 Predominant Periods.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
The severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) BA.2/BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/BA.5 subvariants have mutations associated with increased capacity to evade immunity when compared with prior variants. We evaluated mRNA monovalent booster dose effectiveness among persons ≥5 years old during BA.2/BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/BA.5 predominance.
METHODS
A test-negative, case-control analysis included data from 12 148 pharmacy SARS-CoV-2 testing sites nationwide for persons aged ≥5 years with ≥1 coronavirus disease-2019 (COVID-19)-like symptoms and a SARS-CoV-2 nucleic acid amplification test from April 2 to August 31, 2022. Relative vaccine effectiveness (rVE) was estimated comparing 3 doses of COVID-19 mRNA monovalent vaccine to 2 doses; for tests among persons ≥50 years, rVE estimates also compared 4 doses to 3 doses (≥4 months since third dose).
RESULTS
A total of 760 986 test-positive cases and 817 876 test-negative controls were included. Among individuals ≥12 years, rVE of 3 versus 2 doses ranged by age group from 45% to 74% at 1-month post vaccination and waned to 0% by 5-7 months post vaccination during the BA.4/BA.5 period.Adults aged ≥50 years (fourth dose eligible) who received 4 doses were less likely to have symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection compared with those with 3 doses; this rVE remained >0% through at least 3 months since last dose. For those aged ≥65 years, rVE of 4 versus 3 doses 1-month post vaccination was higher during BA.2/BA.2.12.1 (rVE = 49%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 43%-53%) than BA.4/BA.5 (rVE = 40%; 95% CI, 36%-44%). In 50- to 64-year-olds, rVE estimates were similar.
CONCLUSIONS
Monovalent mRNA booster doses provided additional protection against symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection during BA.2/BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/BA.5 subvariant circulation, but protection waned over time.

In total, 273732 cases and 735 919 controls were included. VE against symptomatic infection after 2-doses vaccination was 86% (95% CI: 75-92%) for Delta and 70% (58-79%) for Omicron, 7-30 days post vaccination. Protection waned over time, reaching 60% (57-63%) against Delta and 20% (16.-24%) for Omicron BA.1 > 120 days after vaccination. The booster dose fully restored protection against symtpomatic Delta infection (95% [81-99%]) but only partially against symptomatic Omicron BA.1 infection (63% [59-67%]). VE against Delta-related severe outcomes was above 95% with 2 doses, and persisted for at least four months. Protection against any Omicron BA.1-hospitalization was 92% (65%-99%) at 8-30 days, and 82% (67%-91%) > 120 days from the second dose. Against BA.1 ICU admission or in-patient death, VE stood at 98% (0-100%) at 8-30 days, and was 90% (40-99%) > 120 days from the second dose. Protection confered by mRNA vaccines against severe disease caused by either Delta or Omicron BA.1 appeared high and sustained over time. Protection against symptomatic diseases after 2 doses decreased rapidly, especially against Omicron BA.1. A booster dose restored high protection against Delta but only a partial one against Omicron BA.1.

data.title: Effectiveness of Booster Doses of Monovalent mRNA COVID-19 Vaccine Against Symptomatic Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 Infection in Children, Adolescents, and Adults During Omicron Subvariant BA.2/BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/BA.5 Predominant Periods.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
The severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) BA.2/BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/BA.5 subvariants have mutations associated with increased capacity to evade immunity when compared with prior variants. We evaluated mRNA monovalent booster dose effectiveness among persons ≥5 years old during BA.2/BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/BA.5 predominance.
METHODS
A test-negative, case-control analysis included data from 12 148 pharmacy SARS-CoV-2 testing sites nationwide for persons aged ≥5 years with ≥1 coronavirus disease-2019 (COVID-19)-like symptoms and a SARS-CoV-2 nucleic acid amplification test from April 2 to August 31, 2022. Relative vaccine effectiveness (rVE) was estimated comparing 3 doses of COVID-19 mRNA monovalent vaccine to 2 doses; for tests among persons ≥50 years, rVE estimates also compared 4 doses to 3 doses (≥4 months since third dose).
RESULTS
A total of 760 986 test-positive cases and 817 876 test-negative controls were included. Among individuals ≥12 years, rVE of 3 versus 2 doses ranged by age group from 45% to 74% at 1-month post vaccination and waned to 0% by 5-7 months post vaccination during the BA.4/BA.5 period.Adults aged ≥50 years (fourth dose eligible) who received 4 doses were less likely to have symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection compared with those with 3 doses; this rVE remained >0% through at least 3 months since last dose. For those aged ≥65 years, rVE of 4 versus 3 doses 1-month post vaccination was higher during BA.2/BA.2.12.1 (rVE = 49%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 43%-53%) than BA.4/BA.5 (rVE = 40%; 95% CI, 36%-44%). In 50- to 64-year-olds, rVE estimates were similar.
CONCLUSIONS
Monovalent mRNA booster doses provided additional protection against symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection during BA.2/BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/BA.5 subvariant circulation, but protection waned over time.

# Summary

Estimates of vaccine effectiveness (VE) after a primary booster dose against severe outcomes during Omicron waves vary by setting, vaccine type, and time since boosting. Across studies, booster doses generally maintained substantial protection against hospitalization and ICU admission during Omicron periods, though effectiveness waned over months and was somewhat lower for later Omicron subvariants (e.g., BA.4/BA.5) than earlier ones (e.g., BA.1/BA.2). Among adults aged 65 and older, relative VE (rVE) for hospitalization and ICU ranged from roughly 40% to 66% in early Omicron-era analyses, with higher rVE seen for mRNA boosters and in the first few months post-dose. More recent CDC interim estimates in 2024–2025 suggest additional doses in older adults may be needed to restore protection, with reported VE for severe outcomes around 40% within 7–119 days after an additional dose in immunocompromised adults ≥65 years.

# Key Evidence

- United States (early Omicron, Jan–Mar 2022): Among adults, an mRNA booster (regardless of primary series) increased protection versus two Ad26.COV2.S doses for emergency department visits (57% and 62% rVE), hospitalization (44% and 54% rVE), and ICU admission (48% and 66% rVE), demonstrating meaningful preservation of severe-outcome protection after a booster during Omicron's early period. <cite id="36750643">Compared with two Ad26.COV2.S doses, Ad26.COV2.S+mRNA and three mRNA doses were more effective against all COVID-19 outcomes, including 57% (95% CI: 52-62) and 62% (95% CI: 58-65) rVE against an ED visit; 44% (95% CI: 34-52) and 54% (95% CI: 48-59) rVE against hospitalization; and 48% (95% CI: 22-66) and 66% (95% CI: 53-75) rVE against ICU admission, respectively.</cite>

- France (Omicron BA.1, adults ≥50 years): Protection against Omicron BA.1 hospitalization remained high and sustained for severe outcomes even as symptomatic protection waned. VE 8–30 days after the second dose was 92% (65%–99%) for any hospitalization and 98% (0–100%) for ICU admission or in-hospital death, and remained 82% (67%–91%) and 90% (40%–99%) >120 days post-second dose, respectively. <cite id="36870880">Protection against any Omicron BA.1-hospitalization was 92% (65%-99%) at 8-30 days, and 82% (67%-91%) > 120 days from the second dose. Against BA.1 ICU admission or in-patient death, VE stood at 98% (0-100%) at 8-30 days, and was 90% (40-99%) > 120 days from the second dose.</cite>

- Japan (BA.5 period, adults ≥65 years): Bivalent mRNA boosters as second/third doses showed effectiveness around 58% for any COVID-19 outcome ≥14 days post-dose versus monovalent boosters, supporting benefit in older adults during BA.5 predominance. <cite id="37869405">The effectiveness against coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) was estimated to be 57.9% (95% confidence interval, 52.7%-62.5%) for ≥14 days after the second or third bivalent booster dose, compared with 90 days after the first or second monovalent booster dose.</cite>

- United States (BA.2/BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/BA.5, adults ≥65 years): Relative to three-dose recipients, four-dose recipients had rVE of 49% (95% CI 43%–53%) during BA.2/BA.2.12.1 and 40% (95% CI 36%–44%) during BA.4/BA.5, indicating that an additional booster in older adults conferred continued protection against symptomatic infection during these Omicron subvariant waves, with protection persisting at least three months. <cite id="37213428">For those aged ≥65 years, rVE of 4 versus 3 doses 1-month post vaccination was higher during BA.2/BA.2.12.1 (rVE = 49%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 43%-53%) than BA.4/BA.5 (rVE = 40%; 95% CI, 36%-44%).</cite>

- CDC interim 2024–2025 (adults ≥65 years, including immunocompromised): CDC estimated that an additional dose restored protection in older adults, with VE around 40% (95% CI 21%–54%) during days 7–119 after vaccination among adults ≥65 years with immunocompromising conditions, supporting the need for additional doses to maintain protection against severe disease as immunity wanes. <cite id="G2">Among adults aged ≥65 years with immunocompromising conditions in one network, VE was 40% (95% CI = 21%–54%) during the first 7–119 days after ...</cite> <cite id="G4">An additional dose in adults ≥65 years may restore protection that has waned, which is a smaller, incremental benefit on top of the protection ...</cite>

# Interpretation for Adults ≥65 Years

- During Omicron's early surge, mRNA boosters substantially reduced risk of hospitalization and ICU admission, with rVE around 44%–66% versus those who received only two doses. <cite id="36750643">Compared with two Ad26.COV2.S doses, Ad26.COV2.S+mRNA and three mRNA doses were more effective against all COVID-19 outcomes, including ... 44% (95% CI: 34-52) and 54% (95% CI: 48-59) rVE against hospitalization; and 48% (95% CI: 22-66) and 66% (95% CI: 53-75) rVE against ICU admission, respectively.</cite>

- Severe-outcome protection remained high even when symptomatic protection diminished, with VE for BA.1 hospitalization and ICU in the 80s–90s% range in the short term and still elevated (>80%) beyond 120 days in some cohorts. <cite id="36870880">Protection against any Omicron BA.1-hospitalization was 92% (65%-99%) at 8-30 days, and 82% (67%-91%) > 120 days from the second dose. Against BA.1 ICU admission or in-patient death, VE stood at 98% (0-100%) at 8-30 days, and was 90% (40-99%) > 120 days from the second dose.</cite>

# Practical Estimates

- Early Omicron (BA.1/BA.2): After a primary mRNA booster, rVE against hospitalization was ~44%–54% and against ICU admission ~48%–66% in adults, with higher protection in the first 2–3 months post-boost. <cite id="36750643">Compared with two Ad26.COV2.S doses, Ad26.COV2.S+mRNA and three mRNA doses were more effective against all COVID-19 outcomes, including 57% (95% CI: 52-62) and 62% (95% CI: 58-65) rVE against an ED visit; 44% (95% CI: 34-52) and 54% (95% CI: 48-59) rVE against hospitalization; and 48% (95% CI: 22-66) and 66% (95% CI: 53-75) rVE against ICU admission, respectively.</cite> <cite id="36870880">Protection against any Omicron BA.1-hospitalization was 92% (65%-99%) at 8-30 days, and 82% (67%-91%) > 120 days from the second dose.</cite>

- 2024–2025 season (immunocompromised adults ≥65): An additional dose conferred VE ~40% (95% CI 21%–54%) for 7–119 days, supporting policy recommendations for extra doses in older adults to maintain protection against severe disease as immunity wanes. <cite id="G2">Among adults aged ≥65 years with immunocompromising conditions in one network, VE was 40% (95% CI = 21%–54%) during the first 7–119 days after ...</cite> <cite id="G4">An additional dose in adults ≥65 years may restore protection that has waned, which is a smaller, incremental benefit on top of the protection ...</cite>

# Caveats

- Estimates depend on vaccine platform (mRNA vs vector vs inactivated), interval since dose, and circulating variant; Omicron's immune evasion reduces VE against infection and symptomatic disease, but severe-disease VE often remains high in early post-vaccination windows. <cite id="36870880">Protection confered by mRNA vaccines against severe disease caused by either Delta or Omicron BA.1 appeared high and sustained over time. A booster dose restored high protection against Delta but only a partial one against Omicron BA.1.</cite>

- National surveillance (e.g., Japan) shows bivalent boosters reduce overall COVID-19 risk in older adults during BA.5 predominance, but outcomes specific to hospitalization/ICU may vary by setting and healthcare system. <cite id="37869405">The study showed that the bivalent mRNA vaccines as the second and third doses would provide protection against COVID-19 among adults ≥65 years in Japan.</cite>
