<snippet id="39316290">Title: A Cost-Effectiveness Analysis of Axicabtagene Ciloleucel versus Tisagenlecleucel in the Treatment of Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma Based on a Real-World French Registry.
Authors: Ray, Markqayne, Castaigne, Jean-Gabriel, Zang, Alexandra et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Advances in therapy
Abstract: INTRODUCTION
Axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel) and tisagenlecleucel (tisa-cel) are chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapies that were evaluated in third and later line (3L+) relapsed or refractory (r/r) diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) in the ZUMA-1 and JULIET trials, respectively. As of October 2021, the DESCAR-T registry included 729 French patients with 3L+ r/r DLBCL who received axi-cel or tisa-cel. Using these data, propensity score matching was used to conduct an adjusted comparison between axi-cel and tisa-cel. Axi-cel was associated with statistically significant improvements in overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS), and significantly more frequent Grade ≥ 3 immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS), compared with tisa-cel. There was no significant difference in Grade ≥ 3 cytokine release syndrome (CRS). The current analysis assessed the cost-effectiveness of axi-cel versus tisa-cel in the treatment of 3L+ r/r DLBCL using propensity score-matched data from the DESCAR-T registry.
METHODS
A partitioned survival model was used to extrapolate costs and quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) over a lifetime. Survival curves for PFS and OS were based on independent mixture cure models fitted to digitized Kaplan-Meier data for the propensity score-matched DESCAR-T populations. Average duration of intensive care unit stays for each of axi-cel and tisa-cel in DESCAR-T were used to inform adverse event costs. Selected parametric survival distributions were based on clinical expert validation. Utility values were derived from ZUMA-1, and costs were obtained from French registries and published sources. List prices were used for both axi-cel and tisa-cel. Costs and outcomes were discounted at an annual rate of 2.5%.
RESULTS
Axi-cel is associated with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of €15,520 per QALY compared with tisa-cel.
CONCLUSION
Based on explicit willingness-to-pay thresholds applied in Europe, axi-cel is expected to be a cost-effective use of healthcare resources in real-world clinical settings compared with tisa-cel in 3L+ r/r DLBCL.</snippet>
<snippet id="36520440">Title: Cost-effectiveness of Axicabtagene Ciloleucel and Tisagenlecleucel as Second-line or Later Therapy in Relapsed or Refractory Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma.
Authors: Choe, Jee H, Abdel-Azim, Hisham, Padula, William V et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: JAMA network open
Abstract: IMPORTANCE
Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapies are approved as a third-line or later therapy for several hematological malignant neoplasms. Recently, randomized clinical trials have investigated their efficacy as a second-line treatment in high-risk relapsed or refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) compared with salvage chemotherapy followed by hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT).
OBJECTIVE
To evaluate the cost-effectiveness of axicabtagene ciloleucel and tisagenlecleucel vs standard care (SC) as second-line or later therapy for relapsed or refractory DLBCL, from both US health care sector and societal perspectives at a cost-effectiveness threshold of $150 000 per quality-adjusted life-year (QALY).
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS
This economic evaluation assessed cost-effectiveness using a partitioned survival model with 2021 US dollars and QALYs over a lifetime horizon. Model inputs were derived from 2 randomized clinical trials (ZUMA-7 and BELINDA) and published literature. In the trials, patients who did not respond to SC received CAR T cells (treatment switching or crossover), either outside the protocol (ZUMA-7) or as part of the protocol (BELINDA). A separate scenario analysis compared second-line axicabtagene ciloleucel with SC alone without treatment crossover to CAR T cell therapy. Data analysis was performed from December 18, 2021, to September 13, 2022.
EXPOSURES
CAR T cell therapy (axicabtagene ciloleucel and tisagenlecleucel) compared with salvage chemotherapy followed by HSCT.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES
Costs and QALYs were used to derive incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) for the health care sector and societal perspectives. Cost and QALYs were discounted at 3.0% annually. Univariate and multivariate probabilistic sensitivity analysis using 10 000 Monte Carlo simulations were applied to test model uncertainty on the ICER.
RESULTS
Second-line axicabtagene ciloleucel was associated with an ICER of $99 101 per QALY from the health care sector perspective and an ICER of $97 977 per QALY from the societal perspective, while second-line tisagenlecleucel was dominated by SC (incremental costs of $37 803 from the health care sector and $39 480 from the societal perspective with decremental QALY of -0.02). Third-line or later tisagenlecleucel was associated with an ICER of $126 593 per QALY from the health care sector perspective and an ICER of $128 012 per QALY from the societal perspective. Based on the scenario analysis of no treatment switching, second-line axicabtagene ciloleucel yielded an ICER of $216 790 per QALY from the health care sector perspective and an ICER of $218 907 per QALY from the societal perspective, compared with SC. When accounting for patients achieving prolonged progression-free survival who would not incur progression-related costs, in this scenario ICER changed to $125 962 per QALY from the health care sector perspective and $122 931 per QALY from the societal perspective. These results were most sensitive to increased list prices of CAR T cell therapy and QALY losses associated with axicabtagene ciloleucel and tisagenlecleucel.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE
These findings suggest that second-line axicabtagene ciloleucel and third-line or later tisagenlecleucel were cost-effective in treating patients with relapsed or refractory DLBCL at the cost-effectiveness threshold of $150 000 per QALY. However, uncertainty remains regarding the best candidates who would experience value gains from receiving CAR T cell therapy.</snippet>
<snippet id="38953781">Title: A Multicenter Real-life Prospective Study of Axicabtagene Ciloleucel versus Tisagenlecleucel Toxicity and Outcomes in Large B-cell Lymphomas.
Authors: Stella, Federico, Chiappella, Annalisa, Casadei, Beatrice et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Blood cancer discovery
Abstract: This real-world prospective observational study across 21 Italian centers (CART-SIE) compares axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel) and tisagenlecleucel (tisa-cel) outcomes in 485 patients with relapsed/refractory large B-cell lymphoma with baseline characteristics matched by stabilized inverse propensity score weighting. Axi-cel versus tisa-cel had higher all-grade cytokine release syndrome (78.6% vs. 89.3%, P = 0.0017) and neurotoxicity (9.9% vs. 32.2%, P < 0.0001) but also superior progression-free survival (PFS) at 1 year (46.5% vs. 34.1%, P = 0.0009). Even among patients who failed bridging therapy, axi-cel PFS was superior to tisa-cel (37.5% vs. 22.7%, P = 0.0059). Differences in overall survival and high-grade immune toxicities were not significant. The CAR-HEMATOTOX score not only predicted hematologic toxicity but also 1-year survival outcomes (51.5% in CAR-HEMATOTOX high vs. 77.2% in CAR-HEMATOTOX low, P < 0.0001). The predictive utility of CAR-HEMATOTOX in assessing not only toxicity but also outcomes across both CAR T-cell products may guide future risk-stratified management strategies.</snippet>

In contrast, salvage chemoimmunotherapy (e.g., R‑ICE/R‑DHAP) after ASCT yields lower response rates and shorter PFS/OS, though ASCT can confer benefit in selected responders. The net value depends on patient selection, risk of toxicity, and healthcare resource context.

A single‑center retrospective series from Gustave Roussy (2008–2020) reported that among transplant‑eligible RR‑DLBCL patients who failed first‑line salvage chemoimmunotherapy and received second‑line R‑DHAP/R‑ICE, the regimen achieved an objective response rate of 33%, median PFS of 2.1 months, and median OS of 11.4 months. - Comparative meta‑analysis (2372 patients, 8 studies): Axi‑cel showed higher odds of complete response (OR 1.65) and higher 1‑year PFS (OR 0.60). A partitioned survival model using these data estimated axi‑cel at €15,520 per QALY versus tisa‑cel in Europe, suggesting cost‑effectiveness at common willingness‑to‑pay thresholds. <cite id="39316290">Using propensity score matching of 729 French patients with 3L+ r/r DLBCL from the DESCAR-T registry, axi-cel was associated with statistically significant improvements in overall survival and progression-free survival, and significantly more frequent Grade ≥3 immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome compared with tisa-cel, with no significant difference in Grade ≥3 CRS; A partitioned survival model estimated axi-cel associated with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of €15,520 per QALY compared with tisa-cel</cite> In US settings, second‑line axi‑cel was cost‑effective (ICER $99,101/QALY health care sector; $97,977/QALY societal), while second‑line tisa‑cel was dominated by salvage chemotherapy/HSCT due to modest gains and toxicity; third‑line or later tisa‑cel was also cost‑effective (ICER ~$126,593/QALY). Sensitivity analyses emphasized the impact of product prices and QALY losses. <cite id="36520440">Second-line axicabtagene ciloleucel was associated with an ICER of $99,101 per QALY from the health care sector perspective and $97,977 per QALY from the societal perspective, while second-line tisagenlecleucel was dominated by SC; third-line or later tisagenlecleucel was associated with an ICER of $126,593 per QALY from the health care sector perspective; results were sensitive to product prices and QALY losses</cite>

After failure of frontline therapy, patients with relapsed/refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (RR-DLBCL) that does not respond to first-line salvage chemotherapy can be recommended second-line salvage chemotherapy. The available literature in this regard is weak, although many centers routinely offer this type of second-line salvage chemotherapy to their patients.

This retrospective study included transplant-eligible patients with RR-DLBCL treated at Gustave Roussy between January 2008 and April 2020. Eligible patients were those who received second-line salvage chemotherapy using R-DHAP or R-ICE in patients who experienced an insufficient partial response, stable disease, or progressive disease in response to first-line salvage chemoimmunotherapy using an alternative regimen.

Forty-six RR-DLBCL patients received second-line salvage regimen, which yielded an objective response rate of 33%, median progression-free survival of 2.1 months, and overall survival of 11.4 months. CONCLUSION
Second-line salvage chemotherapy with R-DHAP or R-ICE followed by ASCT leads to a favorable outcome in almost one third of patients with RR-DLBCL and offers a median overall survival of approximately 1 year. These data support the administration of second-line salvage chemotherapy followed by ASCT.

The higher toxicity and NRM seen with axi-cel might not counterbalance the overall results, highlighting the need for timely intervention and careful selection of patients, balancing resource utilization and clinical benefit.

data.title: Impact of vein-to-vein time in patients with R/R LBCL treated with axicabtagene ciloleucel.
data.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell products axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel), tisagenlecleucel (tisa-cel), and lisocabtagene maraleucel (liso-cel) are approved for relapsed/refractory (R/R) large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL). Emerging evidence indicates that delayed CAR T-cell infusion, including prolonged time from leukapheresis to infusion, known as vein-to-vein time (V2Vt), may adversely impact clinical outcomes. We conducted a systematic literature review (SLR) and meta-analysis to identify differences in V2Vt in patients with R/R LBCL treated with axi-cel, tisa-cel, or liso-cel. The impact of V2Vt (<28 days vs ≥28 to <40 days vs ≥40 days) on effectiveness and safety outcomes was evaluated in patients treated with axi-cel enrolled in a post-authorization safety study using the Center for International Blood and Marrow Transplant Research data. SLR and meta-analysis showed that patients treated with axi-cel had the shortest median V2Vt (30.6 days) compared with tisa-cel (48.4 days) or liso-cel (35.9 days). Real-world analysis of patients treated with axi-cel demonstrated that V2Vt ≥40 days was associated with significantly lower complete response rate than V2Vt <28 days (odds ratio [OR], 0.61) or ≥28 to <40 days (OR, 0.66) and significantly worse overall survival than V2Vt <28 days (hazard ratio [HR], 1.33) or ≥28 to <40 days (HR, 1.36). Higher prolonged thrombocytopenia rates were observed in patients with axi-cel V2Vt ≥28 to <40 days or ≥40 days compared with <28 days (OR, 1.44 or 1.95, respectively). Together, these results show the impact of V2Vt on patient outcomes with axi-cel therapy and that earlier infusion with CD19-CAR therapies may be beneficial.

data.title: A Cost-Effectiveness Analysis of Axicabtagene Ciloleucel versus Tisagenlecleucel in the Treatment of Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma Based on a Real-World French Registry.
data.abstract:
INTRODUCTION
Axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel) and tisagenlecleucel (tisa-cel) are chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapies that were evaluated in third and later line (3L+) relapsed or refractory (r/r) diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) in the ZUMA-1 and JULIET trials, respectively. As of October 2021, the DESCAR-T registry included 729 French patients with 3L+ r/r DLBCL who received axi-cel or tisa-cel. Using these data, propensity score matching was used to conduct an adjusted comparison between axi-cel and tisa-cel. Axi-cel was associated with statistically significant improvements in overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS), and significantly more frequent Grade ≥ 3 immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS), compared with tisa-cel. There was no significant difference in Grade ≥ 3 cytokine release syndrome (CRS). The current analysis assessed the cost-effectiveness of axi-cel versus tisa-cel in the treatment of 3L+ r/r DLBCL using propensity score-matched data from the DESCAR-T registry.
METHODS
A partitioned survival model was used to extrapolate costs and quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) over a lifetime. Survival curves for PFS and OS were based on independent mixture cure models fitted to digitized Kaplan-Meier data for the propensity score-matched DESCAR-T populations. Average duration of intensive care unit stays for each of axi-cel and tisa-cel in DESCAR-T were used to inform adverse event costs. Selected parametric survival distributions were based on clinical expert validation. Utility values were derived from ZUMA-1, and costs were obtained from French registries and published sources. List prices were used for both axi-cel and tisa-cel. Costs and outcomes were discounted at an annual rate of 2.5%.
RESULTS
Axi-cel is associated with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of €15,520 per QALY compared with tisa-cel.
CONCLUSION
Based on explicit willingness-to-pay thresholds applied in Europe, axi-cel is expected to be a cost-effective use of healthcare resources in real-world clinical settings compared with tisa-cel in 3L+ r/r DLBCL.

data.title: Cost-effectiveness of Axicabtagene Ciloleucel and Tisagenlecleucel as Second-line or Later Therapy in Relapsed or Refractory Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma.
data.abstract:
IMPORTANCE
Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapies are approved as a third-line or later therapy for several hematological malignant neoplasms. Recently, randomized clinical trials have investigated their efficacy as a second-line treatment in high-risk relapsed or refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) compared with salvage chemotherapy followed by hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT).
OBJECTIVE
To evaluate the cost-effectiveness of axicabtagene ciloleucel and tisagenlecleucel vs standard care (SC) as second-line or later therapy for relapsed or refractory DLBCL, from both US health care sector and societal perspectives at a cost-effectiveness threshold of $150 000 per quality-adjusted life-year (QALY).
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS
This economic evaluation assessed cost-effectiveness using a partitioned survival model with 2021 US dollars and QALYs over a lifetime horizon. Model inputs were derived from 2 randomized clinical trials (ZUMA-7 and BELINDA) and published literature. In the trials, patients who did not respond to SC received CAR T cells (treatment switching or crossover), either outside the protocol (ZUMA-7) or as part of the protocol (BELINDA). A separate scenario analysis compared second-line axicabtagene ciloleucel with SC alone without treatment crossover to CAR T cell therapy. Data analysis was performed from December 18, 2021, to September 13, 2022.
EXPOSURES
CAR T cell therapy (axicabtagene ciloleucel and tisagenlecleucel) compared with salvage chemotherapy followed by HSCT.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES
Costs and QALYs were used to derive incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) for the health care sector and societal perspectives. Cost and QALYs were discounted at 3.0% annually. Univariate and multivariate probabilistic sensitivity analysis using 10 000 Monte Carlo simulations were applied to test model uncertainty on the ICER.
RESULTS
Second-line axicabtagene ciloleucel was associated with an ICER of $99 101 per QALY from the health care sector perspective and an ICER of $97 977 per QALY from the societal perspective, while second-line tisagenlecleucel was dominated by SC (incremental costs of $37 803 from the health care sector and $39 480 from the societal perspective with decremental QALY of -0.02). Third-line or later tisagenlecleucel was associated with an ICER of $126 593 per QALY from the health care sector perspective and an ICER of $128 012 per QALY from the societal perspective. Based on the scenario analysis of no treatment switching, second-line axicabtagene ciloleucel yielded an ICER of $216 790 per QALY from the health care sector perspective and an ICER of $218 907 per QALY from the societal perspective, compared with SC. When accounting for patients achieving prolonged progression-free survival who would not incur progression-related costs, in this scenario ICER changed to $125 962 per QALY from the health care sector perspective and $122 931 per QALY from the societal perspective. These results were most sensitive to increased list prices of CAR T cell therapy and QALY losses associated with axicabtagene ciloleucel and tisagenlecleucel.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE
These findings suggest that second-line axicabtagene ciloleucel and third-line or later tisagenlecleucel were cost-effective in treating patients with relapsed or refractory DLBCL at the cost-effectiveness threshold of $150 000 per QALY. However, uncertainty remains regarding the best candidates who would experience value gains from receiving CAR T cell therapy.

data.title: A Multicenter Real-life Prospective Study of Axicabtagene Ciloleucel versus Tisagenlecleucel Toxicity and Outcomes in Large B-cell Lymphomas.
data.abstract: This real-world prospective observational study across 21 Italian centers (CART-SIE) compares axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel) and tisagenlecleucel (tisa-cel) outcomes in 485 patients with relapsed/refractory large B-cell lymphoma with baseline characteristics matched by stabilized inverse propensity score weighting. Axi-cel versus tisa-cel had higher all-grade cytokine release syndrome (78.6% vs. 89.3%, P = 0.0017) and neurotoxicity (9.9% vs. 32.2%, P < 0.0001) but also superior progression-free survival (PFS) at 1 year (46.5% vs. 34.1%, P = 0.0009). Even among patients who failed bridging therapy, axi-cel PFS was superior to tisa-cel (37.5% vs. 22.7%, P = 0.0059). Differences in overall survival and high-grade immune toxicities were not significant. The CAR-HEMATOTOX score not only predicted hematologic toxicity but also 1-year survival outcomes (51.5% in CAR-HEMATOTOX high vs. 77.2% in CAR-HEMATOTOX low, P < 0.0001). Twenty patients developed second primary malignancies, including two cases of T-cell neoplasms. These findings enable more informed selection of anti-CD19 CAR T-cell therapy, balancing bridging, safety, and efficacy considerations for individual patients. Significance: The findings of this study on 485 patients with relapsed/refractory large B-cell lymphoma treated with commercial axi-cel and tisa-cel indicate axi-cel's superior PFS after propensity score weighting. The predictive utility of CAR-HEMATOTOX in assessing not only toxicity but also outcomes across both CAR T-cell products may guide future risk-stratified management strategies.

trajectory.final_answer:
# Summary

In relapsed/refractory diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma (DLBCL), CD19‑directed CAR‑T cell therapy (axi‑cel and tisa‑cel) demonstrates superior efficacy to salvage chemoimmunotherapy followed by autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT), with markedly higher complete response and 1‑year progression‑free survival (PFS) rates and numerically higher overall survival (OS), but with greater toxicity (CRS, ICANS, and hematologic toxicity) and higher resource utilization. In contrast, salvage chemoimmunotherapy (e.g., R‑ICE/R‑DHAP) after ASCT yields lower response rates and shorter PFS/OS, though ASCT can confer benefit in selected responders. The net value depends on patient selection, risk of toxicity, and healthcare resource context.

# Evidence for Salvage Chemoimmunotherapy Followed by ASCT

A single‑center retrospective series from Gustave Roussy (2008–2020) reported that among transplant‑eligible RR‑DLBCL patients who failed first‑line salvage chemoimmunotherapy and received second‑line R‑DHAP/R‑ICE, the regimen achieved an objective response rate of 33%, median PFS of 2.1 months, and median OS of 11.4 months. Of 46 patients, 12 proceeded to ASCT; 70% were alive at 1 year post‑ASCT, and multivariable analysis suggested ASCT was associated with improved PFS (HR 0.16) and OS (HR 0.27), supporting the strategy of second‑line salvage chemotherapy followed by ASCT in a subset of patients. <cite id="33277224">After failure of frontline therapy, patients with relapsed/refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (RR-DLBCL) that does not respond to first-line salvage chemotherapy can be recommended second-line salvage chemotherapy; Forty-six RR-DLBCL patients received second-line salvage regimen, which yielded an objective response rate of 33%, median progression-free survival of 2.1 months, and overall survival of 11.4 months; Twelve patients proceeded to autologous stem-cell transplantation (ASCT), of whom 70% remained alive 1 year after ASCT; ASCT was associated with progression-free survival (hazard ratio = 0.16; 95% confidence interval, 0.06-0.42) and overall survival (hazard ratio = 0.27; 95% confidence interval, 0.08-0.88)</cite>

# Evidence for CD19‑directed CAR‑T (Axi‑cel vs Tisa‑cel)

- Comparative meta‑analysis (2372 patients, 8 studies): Axi‑cel showed higher odds of complete response (OR 1.65) and higher 1‑year PFS (OR 0.60). OS appeared improved (OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.68–1.02), while nonrelapse mortality was higher with axi‑cel (11.5%) than tisa‑cel (3.7%). Predictors of survival included LDH, ECOG, and bridging response; axi‑cel maintained superiority in the elderly. Safety signals favored tisa‑cel for grade ≥3 CRS, but axi‑cel had higher odds of any‑grade CRS (OR 3.23), severe ICANS (grade ≥3; OR 4.03), and severe neutropenia at 1 month (OR 2.06), with greater resource utilization (longer hospital stay, ICU admission, tocilizumab use). <cite id="38281590">Axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel) and tisagenlecleucel (tisa-cel) are CD19-directed chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR-T) therapies approved for relapsed/refractory aggressive large B cell lymphoma (LBCL); Axi-cel showed higher odds for a complete response (OR, 1.65; P < .001) and was associated with higher odds for PFS at 1 year after infusion (OR, .60; P < .001); OS appeared to be improved with axi-cel (OR, .84; 95% CI, .68 to 1.02; P = .08), whereas the cumulative incidence of nonrelapse mortality (NRM) was 11.5% for axi-cel versus 3.7% for tisa-cel (P = .002); Axi-cel was associated with significantly higher odds of any-grade CRS (OR, 3.23; P < .001) and severe ICANS (OR, 4.03; P < .001), and higher odds of severe neutropenia (OR, 2.06; P = .003), with greater resource utilization</cite>

- Cost‑effectiveness analyses: In propensity‑matched French registry data (3L+ r/r DLBCL), axi‑cel improved OS and PFS versus tisa‑cel but with significantly more frequent grade ≥3 ICANS; no significant difference in grade ≥3 CRS. A partitioned survival model using these data estimated axi‑cel at €15,520 per QALY versus tisa‑cel in Europe, suggesting cost‑effectiveness at common willingness‑to‑pay thresholds. <cite id="39316290">Using propensity score matching of 729 French patients with 3L+ r/r DLBCL from the DESCAR-T registry, axi-cel was associated with statistically significant improvements in overall survival and progression-free survival, and significantly more frequent Grade ≥3 immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome compared with tisa-cel, with no significant difference in Grade ≥3 CRS; A partitioned survival model estimated axi-cel associated with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of €15,520 per QALY compared with tisa-cel</cite> In US settings, second‑line axi‑cel was cost‑effective (ICER $99,101/QALY health care sector; $97,977/QALY societal), while second‑line tisa‑cel was dominated by salvage chemotherapy/HSCT due to modest gains and toxicity; third‑line or later tisa‑cel was also cost‑effective (ICER ~$126,593/QALY). Sensitivity analyses emphasized the impact of product prices and QALY losses. <cite id="36520440">Second-line axicabtagene ciloleucel was associated with an ICER of $99,101 per QALY from the health care sector perspective and $97,977 per QALY from the societal perspective, while second-line tisagenlecleucel was dominated by SC; third-line or later tisagenlecleucel was associated with an ICER of $126,593 per QALY from the health care sector perspective; results were sensitive to product prices and QALY losses</cite>

- Real‑world multicenter study (485 patients, 1:1 matched): Axi‑cel versus tisa‑cel showed higher all‑grade CRS and neurotoxicity but superior 1‑year PFS (46.5% vs 34.1%), with similar outcomes even among patients who failed bridging therapy; differences in OS and high‑grade immune toxicities were not significant. A prognostic score (CAR‑HEMATOTOX) predicted both hematologic toxicity and 1‑year survival. <cite id="38953781">A real-world prospective observational study across 21 Italian centers compared axi-cel and tisa-cel in 485 relapsed/refractory large B-cell lymphoma patients; axi-cel had higher all-grade CRS and neurotoxicity but superior 1-year PFS (46.5% vs 34.1%), with similar OS and high-grade immune toxicities not significantly different; CAR-HEMATOTOX predicted toxicity and 1-year survival</cite>

- Timing to infusion matters: In axi‑cel recipients, longer vein‑to‑vein time (≥40 days) was associated with lower complete response and worse OS, and higher prolonged thrombocytopenia, supporting the importance of timely delivery to maximize efficacy and minimize toxicity. <cite id="39883946">Real-world analysis of patients treated with axicabtagene ciloleucel demonstrated that V2Vt ≥40 days was associated with significantly lower complete response rate and worse overall survival compared with shorter V2Vt, and higher prolonged thrombocytopenia with longer V2Vt</cite>

# Comparative Interpretation

- Efficacy: Salvage chemoimmunotherapy (R‑ICE/R‑DHAP) after ASCT yields modest response rates and short median PFS/OS, whereas CD19 CAR‑T achieves substantially higher CR rates and 1‑year PFS, with numerically higher OS and favorable cost‑effectiveness in selected settings. <cite id="33277224,38281590,36520440">Second-line salvage chemoimmunotherapy yielded an objective response rate of 33%, median PFS 2.1 months, and OS 11.4 months; axi-cel showed higher odds of complete response and 1-year PFS; second-line axicabtagene ciloleucel was cost-effective with improved outcomes</cite>

- Safety and utilization: CD19 CAR‑T carries higher risks of ICANS and CRS (particularly any‑grade for axi‑cel) and more hematologic toxicity, requiring ICU admission, longer hospitalization, and biologic support (e.g., tocilizumab), which increases healthcare resource use. <cite id="38281590">Axi-cel was associated with higher resource utilization, including prolonged hospital stay, ICU admission, and tocilizumab use, driven by higher CRS and ICANS risks</cite> Real‑world data corroborate higher neurotoxicity and CRS with axi‑cel versus tisa‑cel, though OS differences were not significant in one large matched cohort. <cite id="38953781">Axi-cel had higher neurotoxicity and CRS than tisa-cel but similar overall survival in a matched cohort</cite>

- Patient selection and logistics: Outcomes with CAR‑T are sensitive to timing from apheresis to infusion; shorter vein‑to‑vein time is associated with better CR and survival, underscoring the need for coordinated logistics. <cite id="39883946">V2Vt ≥40 days with axi-cel was linked to lower complete response and worse OS, supporting earlier infusion</cite> Cost‑effectiveness is favorable for second‑line axi‑cel and third‑line or later tisa‑cel in many models, but depends on price, toxicity burden, and QALY impacts. <cite id="36520440,39316290">Second-line axicabtagene ciloleucel and third-line or later tisagenlecleucel were cost-effective in relapsed/refractory DLBCL, with sensitivity to product prices and toxicity</cite>

# Bottom Line

For transplant‑eligible RR‑DLBCL, salvage chemoimmunotherapy followed by ASCT offers limited efficacy with short progression‑free survival, whereas CD19‑directed CAR‑T provides superior disease control and cost‑effectiveness in many scenarios, albeit with higher toxicity and resource demands. Careful patient selection, prompt infusion logistics, and risk‑stratified management (e.g., CAR‑HEMATOTOX) are key to optimizing benefit–risk. <cite id="33277224,38281590,36520440,38953781,39883946">Salvage chemoimmunotherapy followed by ASCT yielded modest responses and short survival; CD19 CAR-T showed higher CR and 1-year PFS, with cost-effectiveness in many settings and higher toxicity/resource use; real-world data support axi-cel's PFS advantage and the importance of timely infusion</cite>
